chapters.title: Book I
paragraphs: Sing, Heavenly Muse, of humanity's first act of disobedience and the fruit of that forbidden tree. Its deadly taste brought death into the world, along with all our suffering and the loss of Eden. Sing until one greater Man restores us and wins back that blessed place. You who inspired that shepherd on the secret peak of Horeb, or Sinai, and first taught the chosen people how the heavens and earth rose out of Chaos -- or if the hill of Zion delights you more, and Siloam's brook that flowed beside God's oracle -- from there I call on your help for my daring song.

It aims to soar beyond any middle flight, above the heights of Helicon, pursuing things never yet attempted in prose or verse. And above all, O Spirit, who prefers an upright and pure heart over any temple, teach me. You know all things. You were present from the very beginning.
With mighty wings spread wide, you brooded like a dove over the vast Abyss and made it fruitful.
Illuminate what is dark in me. Raise and support what is low. So that, rising to the height of this great subject, I may assert God's eternal providence and justify the ways of God to humanity.

Tell me first -- for Heaven hides nothing from your sight, nor does the deep reach of Hell -- tell me what cause moved our first parents, in that happy state so highly favored by Heaven, to fall away from their Creator and break his will over a single restriction, when they were lords of the entire world besides. Who first seduced them into that terrible revolt? It was the infernal Serpent. His cunning, driven by envy and revenge, deceived the mother of all humanity. His pride had already cast him out of Heaven, along with his entire host of rebel angels.

With their help, aspiring to set himself in glory above his peers, he had trusted he could equal the Most High. He opposed God and raised wicked war in Heaven with ambitious aim against the throne and monarchy of God, battling proudly but in vain. The Almighty Power hurled him headlong, flaming, from the ethereal sky, down with hideous ruin and burning destruction to bottomless perdition.

There he would dwell in unbreakable chains and punishing fire -- he who dared defy the Omnipotent to battle. For nine times the span that measures day and night for mortal beings, he and his terrible crew lay defeated, rolling in the fiery gulf. They were stunned, though immortal. But his punishment reserved him for even greater wrath. Now the thought of both lost happiness and unending pain tormented him.

He cast his sorrowful eyes around, eyes that showed immense suffering and despair, mixed with stubborn pride and unwavering hatred. At once, as far as angelic vision could reach, he surveyed the dismal, desolate, wild landscape.

It was a horrible dungeon, flaming on all sides like one great furnace. Yet from those flames came no light. Instead, a visible darkness served only to reveal scenes of misery -- regions of sorrow, mournful shadows where peace and rest could never dwell, where hope that comes to all others never comes. Only endless torture persisted, fed by a fiery flood of ever-burning sulfur that was never consumed. Such a place Eternal Justice had prepared for those rebels. Here their prison was ordained in utter darkness, their fate set as far removed from God and the light of Heaven as three times the distance from the earth's center to the outermost edge of the sky. How unlike the place from which they fell! There Satan soon spotted the companions of his downfall, overwhelmed by floods and whirlwinds of raging fire. Wallowing beside him was the one next to himself in power and next in crime, long afterward known in Palestine and named Beelzebub. To him the Arch-Enemy, called Satan in Heaven, broke the horrible silence with bold words: "If you are truly he -- but oh, how fallen! How changed from the one who, in the happy realms of light, clothed in transcendent brightness, outshone countless others, though they too were bright!

If he with whom I was united in league, in shared thoughts and counsels, in equal hope and danger in our glorious enterprise, is now joined with me in equal ruin -- into what pit you can see we have fallen, from what height. So much stronger his thunder proved. Until then, who knew the force of those terrible weapons?

Yet I do not repent or change, despite those weapons or whatever else the mighty Victor in his rage can inflict. Though changed in outward appearance, my fixed mind remains the same, along with my high disdain born from a sense of injured merit. That disdain raised me to contend with the Mightiest and brought along innumerable armed spirits to the fierce conflict.

They dared to oppose his reign, preferring me. With opposing power, they challenged his supreme might in uncertain battle on the plains of Heaven and shook his throne. What if the battle is lost? Not everything is lost. The unconquerable will remains, and the determination for revenge, immortal hatred, and the courage never to submit or yield. What else is there that cannot be overcome? That glory his wrath or might shall never force from me. To bow and beg for mercy on suppliant knee, to worship the power of one who, because of the terror of this very arm, so recently doubted his own empire -- that would be truly degrading.

That would be a disgrace beneath even this downfall. Since by fate the strength of gods and this heavenly substance cannot fail, and since through the experience of this great conflict, with arms no worse and foresight much improved, we may with better hope resolve to wage eternal war, by force or cunning, against our great Enemy who now triumphs and in his excessive joy holds sole tyrannical rule over Heaven."
So spoke the fallen angel, though in pain, boasting loudly but racked with deep despair.

His bold companion soon answered him: "O Prince, O Chief of many throned Powers who led the battle-ready Seraphim to war under your command, and who in fearless, dreadful deeds endangered Heaven's eternal King and put his supreme authority to the test -- whether upheld by strength, chance, or fate -- I see too well and mourn the terrible outcome.

Our sad defeat has cost us Heaven and laid this mighty host low in horrible destruction, as far as gods and heavenly beings can be destroyed. For the mind and spirit remain unconquerable, and strength soon returns, though all our glory is extinguished and our happy state swallowed up in endless misery. But what if our Conqueror -- whom I now must believe is truly almighty, since nothing less could have overpowered such a force as ours -- has left us our spirit and strength intact, only so we may endure and sustain our pain enough to satisfy his vengeful anger?
Or perhaps to do him mightier service as his slaves by right of conquest, whatever his purpose may be, here in the heart of Hell, working in fire, or running his errands in the gloomy Deep?

What good does it do us then, though we still feel our strength undiminished, or our eternal existence, if it only means undergoing eternal punishment?" To this the Arch-Fiend quickly replied: "Fallen Cherub, to be weak is miserable whether one acts or suffers.

But be sure of this: doing anything good will never be our task. Our sole delight will always be doing evil, since we are the opposite of his high will, which we resist. If his providence then seeks to bring good out of our evil, our work must be to corrupt that purpose and still find ways to bring evil out of good. This may often succeed well enough to grieve him, if I am not mistaken, and disturb his innermost plans from their intended aim.

But look! The angry Victor has called back his ministers of vengeance and pursuit to the gates of Heaven. The sulfurous hail that was shot after us in the storm has died down and stilled the fiery surge that caught us falling from Heaven's edge.

The thunder, winged with red lightning and furious rage, has perhaps spent its bolts and now ceases to roar through the vast, boundless Deep. Let us not miss this opportunity, whether scorn or satisfied fury makes our Enemy yield it to us. Do you see that dreary, forsaken, wild plain, that seat of desolation, empty of light except for what these flickering pale flames dimly cast? Let us head there, away from the tossing of these fiery waves.

There we can rest, if any rest can be found there. We can reassemble our battered forces and plan how to cause our enemy the most harm, how to repair our own losses, how to overcome this terrible disaster, what hope of reinforcement we may gain -- or if not hope, what determination we may draw from despair." So Satan spoke to his nearest companion, with his head lifted above the waves and eyes that blazed with sparks. The rest of his body lay stretched out on the flood, floating for a vast distance, as huge in bulk as the giants of myth and legend -- Briareos or Typhon, whom the cave near ancient Tarsus held, or that sea-beast Leviathan, which God created as the hugest creature that swims the ocean.

Sailors tell that sometimes a pilot of some small, night-lost boat mistakes Leviathan, sleeping on the waters off Norway, for an island. He drops anchor in its scaly hide and moors alongside while night covers the sea and the wished-for morning is delayed. So stretched out in enormous length, the Arch-Fiend lay chained on the burning lake. He would never have risen from there or lifted his head, except that the will and supreme permission of all-ruling Heaven left him free to pursue his own dark designs. Through repeated crimes he would heap damnation upon himself, while seeking evil for others.

In his rage he would see how all his malice only served to bring forth infinite goodness, grace, and mercy shown to the very humanity he had seduced -- while upon himself, triple confusion, wrath, and vengeance were poured. Suddenly he reared his mighty form upright from the pool.

On each side, the flames were driven backward, their pointing spires sloping away. They rolled in billows, leaving a terrible valley in the middle. Then with wings spread wide, he steered his flight upward, riding the dusky air that felt his unusual weight. At last he landed on dry ground -- if you could call it land, since it burned constantly with solid fire, just as the lake burned with liquid fire.

It looked like the landscape when underground forces tear a hill from Mount Pelorus, or the shattered side of thundering Etna, whose combustible interior, catching fire and fueled by mineral fury, aids the winds and leaves a scorched surface covered in stench and smoke. Such footing the soles of those cursed feet found. His closest companion followed him. Both gloried in having escaped the Stygian flood like gods, by their own recovered strength rather than by the tolerance of higher Power.

"Is this the region, this the soil and climate," said the lost Archangel, "this the place we must exchange for Heaven? This mournful gloom for that celestial light? So be it, since the one who now rules supreme can decide what shall be right. Farthest from him is best, since reason made us equals and only force has made him supreme.

Farewell, happy fields where joy forever dwells! Hail, horrors! Hail, infernal world! And you, deepest Hell, receive your new master -- one who brings a mind that will not be changed by place or time. The mind is its own place, and in itself can make a Heaven of Hell, a Hell of Heaven.

What does it matter where I am, if I am still the same, and all I should be except slightly less than him whom thunder has made greater? Here at least we shall be free. The Almighty has not built this place out of jealousy. He will not drive us away from here. Here we may rule secure. And in my judgment, to rule is worth the ambition, even in Hell. Better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven. But why do we leave our faithful friends, our partners in loss, lying stunned on that pool of oblivion?

Why not call them to share their part in this unhappy dwelling, or once more take up arms and try what may yet be regained in Heaven, or what more may be lost in Hell?" So Satan spoke, and Beelzebub answered him: "Leader of those bright armies which none but the Almighty could have defeated!

If they once hear that voice -- their strongest pledge of hope in times of fear and danger, heard so often at the worst extremes and on the perilous edge of battle when it raged most fiercely, their surest rallying signal -- they will soon recover new courage and revive.

Even now they lie groveling and flattened on that lake of fire, as we ourselves lay just moments ago, stunned and dazed. No wonder, after falling from such a tremendous height!" He had barely finished speaking when the greater Fiend was already moving toward the shore.

His enormous shield, forged of ethereal material, massive, large, and round, hung behind him on his shoulders. Its broad circumference was like the moon as seen through a telescope by the Tuscan astronomer Galileo, observing from the hilltop of Fiesole or in the Arno valley, trying to spot new lands, rivers, or mountains on its spotted surface.

His spear -- compared to which the tallest pine hewn on Norwegian hills to serve as the mast of some great flagship would be merely a stick -- he used as a walking staff to support his unsteady steps over the burning ground.
These steps were nothing like his former strides on Heaven's azure floor. The scorching climate struck him hard besides, vaulted all around with fire.
Nevertheless he endured, until he stood on the beach of that flaming sea and called to his legions.

These angel forms lay in a trance, thick as autumn leaves that cover the streams in the shady valley of Vallombrosa beneath the arching Tuscan forests -- or like scattered seaweed floating when fierce winds stirred by Orion have churned the Red Sea coast, the same waves that once overwhelmed Pharaoh and his Egyptian cavalry while they treacherously pursued the Israelites of Goshen, who watched from the safe shore as the floating bodies and broken chariot wheels drifted past.

Just as thickly scattered, ruined and lost, these fallen angels lay covering the flood, dazed by their hideous transformation. He called so loudly that all the hollow depths of Hell echoed: "Princes, Potentates, Warriors, the Flower of Heaven -- once yours, now lost!

Can such astonishment seize eternal spirits? Or have you chosen this place to rest after the hardship of battle, finding such comfort here that you slumber as if in the valleys of Heaven? Or in this humiliating position, have you sworn to worship the Conqueror, who now sees Cherub and Seraph rolling in the flood with scattered weapons and banners?

Soon his swift pursuers will spot the advantage from Heaven's gates and descend to trample us while we lie here helpless, or pin us to the bottom of this gulf with linked thunderbolts. Awake! Arise! Or be fallen forever!" They heard, and they were ashamed. They sprang up on their wings, like soldiers caught sleeping on watch who scramble to their feet before they are fully awake, roused by the very person they dread. They clearly saw the terrible situation they were in and felt the fierce pains.
Yet they quickly obeyed their General's voice, innumerable in number.

It was like when the powerful rod of Moses, in Egypt's day of evil, waved along the coast and summoned a dark cloud of locusts, carried on the east wind, that hung over the realm of wicked Pharaoh like night and darkened all the land of the Nile.

Just as countless were those wicked angels, hovering on their wings under the roof of Hell, between the fires above, below, and all around. Then, at a signal given, the uplifted spear of their great leader waved to direct their course. In even formation they descended and landed on the solid brimstone, filling the entire plain. A host so vast that the populous North never poured from its frozen lands such numbers to cross the Rhine or the Danube, when its barbarian hordes came like a flood upon the South and spread beneath Gibraltar all the way to the Libyan sands.

At once, from every squadron and every band, the leaders and commanders hurried to where their great Commander stood. They were godlike figures and forms surpassing human beauty -- princely Dignities and Powers that once sat on thrones in Heaven, though their names in heavenly records were now blotted out and erased because of their rebellion from the Book of Life.

They had not yet gained new names among the sons of Eve. But later, wandering over the earth by God's permission to test humanity, they corrupted most of mankind through lies and deception. They led people to abandon God their Creator and to transform the invisible glory of their Maker into the image of beasts. They adorned these false religions with pomp and gold, and people worshiped devils as deities. Then they became known to humanity by various names, and various idols spread throughout the pagan world. Tell me, Muse, their names as they were later known. Who first, who last, roused from their slumber on that fiery couch at their great Emperor's call, came forward one by one to where he stood on the bare shore, while the undistinguished crowd stood back at a distance?
The chief among them were those who, roaming from the pit of Hell to seek prey on Earth, dared long afterward to set up their altars next to God's altar.

They were gods worshiped among the surrounding nations. They dared to stand against Jehovah thundering from Zion, enthroned between the Cherubim. They even placed their shrines and abominations within his own sanctuary, profaning his holy rites and solemn festivals. With their darkness they dared to confront his light. First was Moloch, that horrifying king, smeared with the blood of human sacrifice and parents' tears. Though the noise of drums and tambourines drowned out the cries of children who were passed through fire to his grim idol. The Ammonites worshiped him in Rabba and its watery plain, in Argob and in Bashan, all the way to the stream of the outermost Arnon. Not content with such bold proximity to God, he led even the wisest heart of Solomon by fraud to build his temple directly opposite the temple of God, on that shameful hill.

He made his grove in the pleasant Valley of Hinnom, which was then called Tophet and Black Gehenna -- the very image of Hell. Next came Chemosh, the obscene dread of Moab's people, worshiped from Aroer to Nebo and the wilderness of southernmost Abarim, in Heshbon and Horonaim, Sihon's realm, beyond the flowery valley of Sibmah covered in vines, and Elealeh all the way to the Dead Sea.
Peor was his other name, when he lured Israel at Shittim during their march from the Nile into performing lustful rites that cost them dearly.
From there he spread his obscene worship even to that hill of scandal, beside the grove of murderous Moloch -- lust right next to hate -- until good King Josiah drove them all back to Hell.

With these came those who, from the bordering waters of the ancient Euphrates to the brook that separates Egypt from Syrian territory, had the general names of Baalim and Ashtaroth -- the males called Baalim, the females Ashtaroth. For spirits can take on either gender, or both.

Their pure essence is so soft and simple, not bound or shackled by joints or limbs, nor dependent on the brittle strength of bones like heavy flesh. In whatever shape they choose, expanded or compressed, bright or dark, they can carry out their purposes and perform works of love or hostility.

For these false gods, the people of Israel often forsook their Living Strength. They abandoned his righteous altar, bowing low to worship bestial gods. For this their heads were bowed just as low in battle, falling before the spears of contemptible enemies. Among these came Astoreth, whom the Phoenicians called Astarte, queen of heaven, with crescent horns.

To her the women of Sidon bowed with moonlit worship. She was seen also in Zion, where her offending shrine stood, built by that heart bewitched by women -- the one who was the wisest of kings. After her came Thammuz, whose annual wound was mourned in Lebanon. The stream that ran with love's blood ran purple to the sea through a seductive spell, while each year smooth Syrian maidens spent a summer's day lamenting his fate.

The love-tale of Thammuz infected Zion's daughters with similar passion. Ezekiel saw them in his vision, weeping for Thammuz at the northern gate of the Lord's house. Next came the one whose name would in later ages inspire the greatest terror -- Dagon, that sea-monster, half man and half fish. His temple was raised in Azotus, dreaded through the coast of Palestine, in Gath, Askelon, Accaron, and Gaza's frontier bounds. He also fell down, and his head and both hands were cut off shamefully on his own threshold.

Dagon lay humiliated on the floor of his own temple, to the scorn of all his worshipers. Next came Rimmon, whose pleasant seat was Damascus on the fertile banks of the Abbana and Pharphar, those bright streams. He also stole a leper's heart, the leprosy of Naaman. He lost a king of Israel as well, who bowed before his idol in the house of Rimmon. The one true God was scorned and had his temple desecrated with vile reproach. After these came a flock of spirits so debased that they took the lowest forms -- Osiris, Isis, Orus, and their followers.

These wandered in borrowed shapes, disguised as monstrous forms with animal heads, yet their maddened worshipers called them gods. Israel did not escape this plague in Oreb. They shaped a golden calf when the rebel king doubled his sin at Bethel and in Dan, equating God with a grazing ox. Jehovah, who had shown himself visibly among them in thunder, lightning, and loud trumpets, was forced to live among their crude idols, beside their bestial gods.

Then came Belial, more wicked than all the rest. No one ever fell more deeply into the love of vice for its own sake. He had no temple built to him and no altar smoked in his honor. Yet who could be more common? His priests filled the temples of God with cursing and deceit. His violence and robbery profaned even the holy of holies. Eli's sons filled the house of God with their lust. He also reigned in the courts and palaces, and in luxurious cities where the noise of revelry rises above the tallest towers. When night darkens the streets, then Belial's sons, inflamed with wine, roam about.

Witness the streets of Sodom, and that night in Gibeah when the laws of hospitality were so shamefully violated that the guest was exposed, and his host offered his virgin daughter to prevent a worse rape. These were the chief among countless others. The Ionian gods too were among them -- those whom Greece called the children of Heaven and Earth, though born later, claiming more fame than they deserved. Titan, Heaven's firstborn, along with his enormous brood, ruled first. Then Saturn, younger born, usurped his brother's throne by the help of Rhea, his wife. Saturn in turn was displaced by the mightier Jove, his own son, who seized his father's throne and cast Saturn down to rule old and feeble in Crete and over the Adriatic to the Hesperian fields and on the Celtic shore.

All these and more came flocking. But their looks were downcast and dampened with dismay, though they claimed to be immortals. Yet they regained some of their lost courage when they saw how their mighty Chief, not broken by his hard fate, stood with undiminished glory, still holding his position as the commanding figure that seemed to carry the weight of highest power.

He appeared like the sun, newly risen, dimmed through horizontal mists -- or like the sun eclipsed behind the moon, shedding an ominous twilight over half the nations, and troubling kings with fears of revolution. So darkened, yet shining above them all, the Arch-angel stood. His face bore deep scars of thunder, and care sat heavy upon his faded cheeks. But underneath his brow, unconquered courage and deliberate pride, resolved and waiting for revenge, were clearly visible.

His eyes displayed cruel resolve, yet mixed with these was pity -- pity for his faithful followers who now deserved a better fate, standing before him in their suffering millions. His attention turned, and three times the tears that angels weep came to his eyes.
He wiped them away, and when he could compose his features, though still marked by the passion of the moment, not lacking angelic dignity, he spoke in a measured voice broken by sighs.

"O countless myriads of immortal spirits, O Powers that only the Almighty could have matched! If that great conflict was not truly ill-advised, then neither was the unchanging boldness and proud determination that hazarded so great a cause, demonstrated by what we did and what we suffered in that battle.

No prediction could have foretold what has happened, or what force was needed to defeat such a force as ours -- though now lost, as far as the might and glory of heaven's inhabitants can be judged lost. Too well I see and mourn how that terrible fall has ruined such a glorious host.

But will our great enemy be reassured by this? Can he believe that I, thus weakened, or the force of these mighty legions, whose exile has emptied Heaven, will ever fail to rise again and reclaim our rightful place? The enemy himself would not wish that. From the terror of this arm they learned their lesson -- not recently, this I freely admit -- and found in me a foe more powerful than they knew. Having learned by experience the full extent of this huge empire, with its sure foundations and its forces armed in strength that equals his, he will choose from here on to wage his wars through cunning rather than open force. We must devise and plan well. This is what a council must decide. For since open war has been rejected -- when was it ever known that celestial spirits bowed to the force of evil? -- we must work through fraud. His kingdom will not long be secure through tyranny." He had barely finished when all the host of Hell raised a tremendous shout that echoed through the hollow deep. They defiantly clashed their shields with loud clanging and beat their swords against them, hurling warlike defiance toward the vault of Heaven.
Nearby stood a hill, not far from the place where they landed. Its grim peak belched fire and rolling smoke. Its shining surface suggested that veins of liquid gold had flowed beneath.

A band, led by Mammon, the least elevated spirit that fell from Heaven -- for even in Heaven his looks and thoughts were always directed downward, admiring the golden pavement more than anything divine or holy that was offered to his sight -- soon opened a vast wound in the hill and dug out ribs of gold.

Let no one marvel at riches growing in Hell. That soil most deserved the most precious ore. These pioneers, with spade and pickaxe armed, soon ransacked the bowels of their mother earth and robbed the center of its hidden treasures -- things better left hidden.

And here let those who boast of mortal accomplishments be admonished. Neither Babel nor the great works of Memphis approached what these demons achieved so easily, in just one hour. Built like a temple, with pilasters of massive gold rising above the columns, the great structure took shape. An architect designed the work. He was well known in Heaven by the name of Mulciber. Stories later told how he was thrown headlong from the crystal battlements by angry Jove. He fell from morning until noon, from noon until dusk, and with the setting sun dropped from his zenith, like a falling star, onto the island of Lemnos in the Aegean Sea. That is how the story goes, but he fell long before, hurled down with the rest of his rebel crew.

Nor did his building arts in Heaven help him, though he had built many a towering structure there. The work rose from the plain like an exhalation, to the sound of harmonious symphonies and sweet voices. It rose, complete with all its ornaments of gold. Nor did those skilled architects of ancient Babylon or Egypt with their greatest efforts build anything to equal it. Nor was Alcairo ever so splendid, or the seat of the great Sultan with its gorgeous towers to entertain the foreign emissaries of the Grand Signior.

The ascending structure now stood fixed at its full height. Its roof was fretted gold. Great doors of gold swung open on their hinges, revealing a vast interior space -- a smooth floor, beyond what many a modern king might boast of as his throne room. Ranks and rows of starry lamps and blazing torches, fed with naphtha and sulfur, cast their light. Crowds flowed in like a swarm from a hive, and marvel of marvels, these vast spirits condensed their huge forms into smaller shapes, reducing their immense stature to the smallest size. They became as numerous as the tiny beings of fairy legend -- the elves or pixies that peasants see, or dream they see, at midnight by a forest's edge or near a fountain, dancing under the waning moon.

The late-night traveler watches, both pleased and fearful, while overhead the moon rides high and casts a paler light on the scene. But far within, in their own dimensions, the great Seraphic lords and Cherubim sat in secret session and close council. A thousand demigods sat on golden seats. After a brief pause, their great leader called a full assembly.

chapters.title: Book II
paragraphs: High on a throne of royal state, which outshone the wealth of Ormuz and of India, or of the Orient's richest treasures scattered upon its barbaric kings, Satan sat, exalted beyond all hope of aspiring higher. Raised to that eminence by merit in the ill venture, he lifted himself to the height of his own bad fortune.

Far from true happiness, his insatiable ambition only raised him higher to make his fall more painful. "Powers, Dominions, and Deities of Heaven!" he began. "No one who claims such thrones in Heaven can rightly call the claim to rule in Hell doubtful.
There is no risk that any one of you, knowing the strength of a tested claim backed by the free choice and vote of all who find themselves here, would want to contest my leadership.

For none who holds such rank in a state so certain would ever envy those who rank higher. But these are not our greatest concerns. "Rather, let us discuss how we may best take advantage of what hope remains from our present situation.
By what strategy or force we may best achieve our own deliverance, or if not victory, then at least revenge."
First, Moloch rose -- the strongest and fiercest spirit that fought in Heaven.
His rage was not diminished by his despair. He now counted nothing lost but revenge.
Trusting in his own strength, he held an attitude of reckless daring and openly defied the Almighty. "My sentence is for open war," he said. "I am not one for tricks.
Let those who need them scheme as they will.
While they sit here deliberating, millions of armed spirits wait outside, longing for the signal to charge.
Should Heaven's exiles sit here hatching empty plots in a dark, dreaded jail shut off from the light, when they could muster their forces and storm the towers of Heaven itself?"

"We should not fear exile. Nothing can be worse than sitting here, suffering fire and torment in this dark bottomless pit. We are already at the lowest point. Fortune cannot sink us lower. Let us then turn our torments into weapons against our tormentor.

Even if we cannot prevail, we can at least disturb his Heaven and mix it with Hell's fire, or if that fails, fill it with such noise and fury that his peace, if he has any, will never be undisturbed again.
This would be no contemptible revenge." When Moloch sat down, Belial rose next.
He was a spirit of more graceful and humane demeanor. He seemed made for high dignity. False eloquence flowed from his tongue.

He could make the worse appear the better cause and turn reason inside out. His thoughts were low, but his speech was lofty. "I should be much in favor of open war, since I agree that sitting here in darkness, stripped of former glory, is not a happy state,"
he said. "But I hear Moloch's plan with alarm. He speaks of leveling Heaven's high towers and forcing our way back to fight.
Who among us saw those towers and knew who sat there would think it possible to storm them by force? Even if we rallied every lost soul in Hell?
The towers of Heaven are filled with armed watchers, unassailable against all attack. "And what of God himself? Shall we provoke the Almighty Victor to unleash his full fury?
He held back before. He left our spirits and strength intact for his own purposes.
He could have ended us entirely. If he did, we would cease to exist.
There would be no us to feel pain or regret. That, I think, would be the worst outcome. "Let me offer a different counsel.

Since our present suffering, though severe, is bearable, and we have already adapted somewhat to these flames, perhaps in time they will grow familiar. Our tempered nature may adjust to them, as it once adjusted to the elements of Heaven. The sharp edge of the fire may soften over endless ages. This is my advice: not war, whether open or concealed. War we have already lost, and further war would only bring worse upon us. Rather, let us live as we are, making the best of our sentence, and hope that in time, our supreme Enemy may relent."
Thus Belial counseled ease and ignoble sloth, not peace. Mammon spoke next.
"Suppose we could gain back Heaven," said Mammon, "what would it profit us? We would have to stand again in the presence of him whom we hate, singing forced praises forever.

This thought is intolerable. How wearisome would eternity be, spent in worship against our will? Let us rather seek our own good from within ourselves and live free in this vast domain, turning what appears evil to our advantage.
Our torments may in time become our elements. This desert soil contains hidden splendors.

We can imitate Heaven's light with our own gems and gold. We can build empires in Hell that rival what Heaven offers, establishing here a kingdom of our own." Mammon finished to what sounded like the murmur of the sea after a storm -- the assembly preferring his counsel of settled peace over desperate war. But Beelzebub, second only to Satan in power, rose to speak.
His commanding presence silenced the hall. "Thrones and Imperial Powers, children of Heaven -- for we are still that, despite our fall," he began.
"We debate here as though we had a choice of peace or war. Let me correct that illusion. The Victor has already decided our fate. He will never restore us. He will not grant us peace.

We are his captives, the conquered inhabitants of this prison house, which his power maintains. "But there is a plan worth considering. There is a place, if ancient prophecy has not failed -- a world recently created, the favorite home of a new race called Man. This creature is less powerful than angels but is highly favored by the Almighty. The new world might prove vulnerable. What if we could corrupt this new creation, seduce or destroy these beings, and thus strike at God through his newest and dearest work?

Whether by force or subtlety, or both, this seems the most promising venture." A murmur of approval ran through the assembly. Every face brightened. Beelzebub continued. "This plan I offer to the council. But who will go? The journey through the void beyond Hell's gates is perilous. Who dares to brave the abyss that separates our prison from that new-created world?" The whole assembly sat silent. No one volunteered.
The danger was too great, the distance too vast, the unknown too terrifying. Then Satan, pleased that none dared what he himself intended, rose with monarchal pride.
"Princes, do not let this great enterprise fail for want of one willing to face its dangers. I will go.
I will not shrink from the attempt, though long the way and hard, through the void immense. I go alone.

None shall share this glory with me, or divide the risk." His speech ended all debate. They rose in admiration of such daring virtue from their fallen prince. Suddenly, both Hell's doors opened with a blast of smoke, revealing the vast chaos beyond. The council dissolved. Some went their separate ways, exploring their new domain.
Groups of fallen angels wandered Hell's geography -- some alongside a river of fire, others on frozen plains, others through regions of perpetual darkness.
Some sat on hills and sang sad songs, lamenting their fate. Others debated philosophy on another hill, reasoning in circles about providence, free will, and fate, but finding no resolution.
Meanwhile Satan approached the massive gates of Hell, which rose to enormous height, guarded by nine layers -- three of brass, three of iron, three of solid diamond.
The flames that surrounded them were impenetrable. At the gate sat two formidable shapes.
One seemed a woman down to the waist, fair and alluring, but ended below in a scaly, serpentine form with a deadly sting.
Around her middle, a pack of hideous Hell-hounds barked ceaselessly, retreating into her womb when alarmed and then emerging again.
The other shape, if it could be called a shape, was a dark, formless thing -- a shadow that seemed both substance and illusion, terrible beyond description.
On its head it wore what seemed a kingly crown. Satan approached undaunted. The shadowy figure moved to block his way.
They stood facing each other, two terrible forms, each measuring the other's strength.
"Where are you going?" the shadow demanded. "Through this gate no one passes without my permission.

I am Death." Satan's fury blazed. "Do not think, foul spirit, that your shape, whatever it is, can prevent me. Stand aside, or face what you have never met before. Go back to whatever filthy pool spawned you!"
They would have clashed then, two monstrous powers shaking all of Hell, had not the woman-serpent rushed between them with a terrible cry. "Father!
Do not raise your hand against your own son! And you -- do not raise yours against your father!" she screamed.
Satan stopped, amazed. "What do you mean? How am I father, and he my son?" She told her story.
She was Sin, born from Satan's head in Heaven when he first conceived the rebellion. Death was their offspring, conceived in an incestuous union.
Now she held the key to Hell's gate, given her by God's own decree. "You are my father, you gave me being," she said. "Whom should I obey but you?

Whom should I follow? You will bring me soon to that new world of light and happiness, among the gods who live at ease, where I shall reign at your right hand in pleasure, as befits your daughter and darling, forever."
With these words, from her side she took the fatal key, the sad instrument of all our woe.

Moving toward the gate, rolling her bestial train, she drew up the huge portcullis that no other power in all of Hell could have moved. She turned the intricate locks, and every bolt and bar of massive iron or solid rock unfastened easily.
The infernal doors flew open with a thunderous crash that shook the lowest foundations of Erebus.
She opened them, but to shut them again was beyond her power.
The gates stood wide open, broad enough for an entire army to march through. They stood so wide, casting forth billowing smoke and ruddy flame like a furnace mouth.
Before their eyes appeared the secrets of the ancient Deep -- a dark, boundless ocean without limit or dimension, where length, breadth, height, time, and place were all lost.
Ancient Night and Chaos, ancestors of Nature, held eternal anarchy there amidst the noise of endless wars and maintained their reign through confusion.
For the four competing elements -- Hot, Cold, Moist, and Dry -- struggled fiercely for dominance there.
Their embryonic atoms swarmed around the banner of each faction. Chaos sat as umpire, but his decisions only embroiled the conflict further. Chance governed everything.
Into this wild Abyss -- the womb of Nature and perhaps her grave -- the wary Fiend stood on the brink of Hell and gazed for a long time, considering his journey.
He had no narrow strait to cross. At last he spread his sail-broad wings for flight. Rising in the surging smoke, he launched himself boldly upward.

But that perch soon failed. He met a vast emptiness and dropped plummeting ten thousand fathoms deep. He would have fallen to this very hour had not a violent, fire-charged cloud caught him and hurled him back up.
That turbulence subsided. He was nearly swallowed in a boggy marsh, neither sea nor solid land. Half on foot, half flying, he struggled onward.

Like a griffin pursuing through the wilderness an Arimaspian who had stolen guarded gold, so eagerly the Fiend pursued his way over bog and cliff, through rough and smooth terrain, with head, hands, wings, or feet -- swimming, sinking, wading, creeping, or flying.
At length a universal wild noise of stunning sounds and confused voices assaulted his ears.

He flew undaunted toward it, seeking whatever Power or Spirit might reside in that noise, from whom he could ask which way the nearest border of darkness lay, bordering on light. There he found the throne of Chaos, with his dark pavilion spread wide over the wasteful Deep. Beside him sat Night, the eldest of all things, the consort of his reign. Around them stood Orcus, Hades, and the dreaded Demogorgon, along with Rumor, Chance, Tumult, Confusion, and Discord with a thousand mouths.
Satan turned boldly to them: "You Powers and Spirits of this nethermost Abyss, Chaos and ancient Night!
I come not as a spy to explore or disturb the secrets of your realm. Forced to wander through this dark desert, my path lies through your vast empire toward the light.
Alone and without a guide, half lost, I seek whatever path leads most directly to where your gloomy borders meet Heaven.
Or, if some other place lately won from your domain is held by the Ethereal King, I travel this depth to reach it.

Direct my course. If I succeed, it brings no small benefit to you. If I reclaim that lost region and restore it to its original darkness and your rule -- which is my present purpose -- I will once more raise the banner of ancient Night there. All the advantage will be yours; all the revenge, mine." So spoke Satan. The old ruler of Chaos answered with faltering speech and uneasy expression: "I know you, stranger.
I know who you are -- that mighty leading angel who recently made war against Heaven's King, though defeated. I saw and heard everything.
For such a vast host did not flee in silence through my frightened realm, with ruin upon ruin, confusion piled on confusion.
Heaven's gates poured out millions of victorious troops in pursuit.
I keep watch here on my frontiers, trying to defend what little remains of my diminishing realm, constantly weakened by internal strife and the encroachments of Hell on one side.
And now recently, Heaven and Earth -- another world -- hang suspended over my realm, linked by a golden chain to the side of Heaven from which your legions fell.

If that is the direction you are heading, it is not far. But the danger is all the greater. Go, and make haste. Havoc, spoil, and ruin are my gain." He stopped speaking. Satan wasted no time on a reply. Glad that his journey across the sea would find a shore at last, he sprang upward with renewed energy, like a pyramid of fire launching into the wild expanse.

Through the shock of fighting elements on every side, he won his way -- harder pressed and more endangered than when Jason's ship Argo passed through the clashing rocks of the Bosporus, or when Odysseus steered between Charybdis on one side and Scylla's whirlpool on the other. With great difficulty and labor he moved on.
But once he had passed, shortly afterward when humanity fell, a strange transformation occurred.

Sin and Death, following his trail as Heaven willed, paved a broad, beaten highway after him over the dark Abyss. Its boiling gulf meekly endured a bridge of tremendous length, stretching from Hell continuously to the outermost edge of this fragile world.

Through it, wicked spirits could pass easily back and forth to tempt or punish mortals, except those whom God and good angels guarded by special grace. But now at last the sacred influence of light appeared.
From the walls of Heaven, it shot far into the heart of dim Night like a glimmering dawn.
Here Nature first began her farthest edge, and Chaos retreated like a broken enemy, with less tumult and less hostile noise.
Satan now traveled more easily on the calmer waves in that uncertain light.

Like a weather-beaten ship that gladly reaches port though its sails and rigging are torn, or like a bird weighing its spread wings in empty air, he paused to gaze at the distant sight of the empyreal Heaven, stretching wide in its circuit, with opal towers and battlements adorned with living sapphire -- once his native home.
And close by, hanging from a golden chain, he saw this pendant World. It was no larger than a star of the smallest size seen next to the moon.
Toward it, fully loaded with mischievous revenge, accursed and in a cursed hour, he hastened.

chapters.title: Book III
paragraphs: Hail, holy Light, firstborn offspring of Heaven, or the eternal beam's coeternal ray! May I express you without blame? Since God is light, and never dwelt except in light beyond all approach, dwelling from eternity in you, bright outpouring of bright essence, uncreated.

Or do you prefer to be called a pure ethereal stream whose fountain no one can trace? Before the sun existed, before the Heavens were made, you already were. At the voice of God, you invested the rising world of dark and deep waters, won back from the void and formless infinite, wrapping it like a mantle.

I revisit you now with bolder wing, having escaped the Stygian pool, though long detained in that dark realm. Through utter and middle darkness I was carried, singing of Chaos and eternal Night with notes quite different from Orpheus's lyre.

Taught by the heavenly Muse to venture down into the dark descent and then to climb back up again, though that journey was hard and rare, I revisit you safely and feel your life-giving, sovereign light. But you do not revisit these eyes of mine, which roll in vain searching for your piercing ray and find no dawn.

So thick a film of blindness has quenched their sight, or dim suffusion veiled them. Yet I do not stop wandering where the Muses dwell -- by clear springs, shady groves, or sunny hills, smitten with the love of sacred song. I visit you nightly, O Zion, and the flowery brooks that wash your hallowed feet and flow with warbling music. Nor do I sometimes forget those other two who shared my fate, if only I could match their fame.

Blind Thamyris, blind Homer, and the prophets Tiresias and Phineus. I feed on thoughts that spontaneously produce harmonious verse, like the nightingale that sings in the dark, hidden in the deepest shade, tuning her nightly song. The seasons return with the year, but day does not return to me, nor the sweet approach of evening or morning, nor the sight of spring blossoms, summer roses, flocks, herds, or the divine human face.

Instead, clouds and everlasting darkness surround me, cutting me off from the cheerful ways of other people. The book of knowledge is presented to me as a universal blank. Nature's works are erased from my sight, and wisdom is shut out at one entrance completely.

Therefore, celestial Light, shine all the more inward. Illuminate the mind through all its powers. Plant eyes within it. Purge and scatter every mist, so that I may see and tell of things invisible to mortal sight.

Now the Almighty Father, from above in the pure heaven of heavens where he sits enthroned above all heights, bent his gaze down to view his own works and their works at once. Around him all the holy beings of Heaven stood thick as stars, receiving from his sight a bliss beyond words. At his right hand sat the radiant image of his glory, his only Son. On earth, he first beheld our two first parents, the only two humans yet alive, placed in the happy garden and enjoying immortal fruits of joy and love -- unbroken joy, unmatched love, in blissful solitude. He then surveyed Hell and the gulf between, and Satan there, coasting the wall of Heaven on the dark side of Night, ready now to descend with weary wings and eager feet onto the bare outside of this world, which seemed like firm land set within the ocean, though it was uncertain whether ocean or air.

God, beholding Satan from his high vantage point where past, present, and future are all visible, spoke to his only Son with foreknowledge: "Only begotten Son, do you see what rage drives our Adversary? No prescribed bounds, no bars of Hell, nor all the chains heaped upon him, nor even the vast main Abyss that lies between, can hold him. So determined he seems on desperate revenge that it shall recoil upon his own rebellious head. And now, having broken through every restraint, he wings his way not far from Heaven, in the borders of light, heading straight for the newly created world and the man placed there. He intends to test whether he can destroy man by force, or worse, pervert him through cunning lies. And he will succeed in perverting him.

For man will listen to his flattering lies and easily break the sole command, the only pledge of his obedience. He will fall, and so will all his faithless descendants. Whose fault will it be? Whose but his own? He was ungrateful. He had everything he could have from me. I made him just and upright, able to stand, though free to fall.

I created all the ethereal Powers and Spirits the same way -- both those who stood firm and those who fell. Those who stood, stood freely. Those who fell, fell by their own choice. If they were not free, what proof could they have given of true loyalty, constant faith, or love? If they could only do what they must do, not what they would choose to do, what praise could they earn?

What pleasure would I receive from such forced obedience, where will and reason -- and reason is also choice -- were rendered useless and empty, both stripped of freedom, both made passive, serving necessity rather than me? They were therefore created as they rightly should have been, and they cannot justly accuse their Maker, or their making, or their fate, as if predestination overruled their will, disposed by absolute decree or by foreknowledge. They themselves decreed their own revolt, not I. Even if I foreknew it, foreknowledge had no influence on their fault. It would have happened just as certainly even if I had not foreseen it.

So without the slightest push from fate, or anything immutably foreseen by me, they trespass. They are authors of all their own choices -- both what they judge and what they choose. For I formed them free, and free they must remain until they enslave themselves. Otherwise I would have to change their nature and revoke the high, unchangeable, eternal decree that ordained their freedom. They ordained their own fall.

The first group fell by their own inclination, self-tempted and self-corrupted. Man falls deceived by the others. Therefore Man shall find grace. The others shall not. In both mercy and justice, through Heaven and Earth, my glory shall shine all the greater.

But Mercy, first and last, shall shine the brightest." While God spoke, an ambrosial fragrance filled all of Heaven. A sense of new and inexpressible joy spread through the blessed spirits. Beyond all comparison, the Son of God appeared most glorious. All his Father shone substantially expressed in him. In his face, divine compassion was visibly apparent -- love without end and grace without measure. Uttering these feelings, he spoke to his Father.

"O Father, gracious was that word which closed your sovereign command -- that Man should find grace. For this, both Heaven and Earth shall highly praise you with innumerable hymns and sacred songs. Your throne shall resound with your blessings forever.

For should Man be finally lost -- should Man, your creature lately so loved, your youngest son, fall circumvented by fraud, though joined with his own folly? Let that be far from you, Father, who are the judge of all things made and judge only rightly.

Or shall the Adversary achieve his end and frustrate yours? Shall he fulfill his malice and bring your goodness to nothing? Shall he return proudly, though to heavier punishment, yet with his revenge accomplished, dragging all of humanity after him to Hell? Or will you yourself abolish your creation and unmake for his sake what you made for your own glory?

If so, both your goodness and your greatness would be questioned and blasphemed without defense." To this the great Creator replied: "O Son, in whom my soul takes its chief delight, Son of my heart, Son who are uniquely mine,

My Word, my Wisdom, and my effective Might -- you have spoken all my thoughts exactly, all as my eternal purpose has decreed. Man shall not be entirely lost. Those who are willing shall be saved. Yet not by their own will, but by grace freely given by me. Once more I will renew his failed powers, though they were forfeited and enslaved by sin to corrupt and excessive desires.
Upheld by me, he shall once more stand on even ground against his mortal enemy. Upheld by me, so that he may know how frail his fallen condition is and owe all his deliverance to me alone.

Some I have chosen by special grace, elected above the rest. That is my will. The rest shall hear my call and be warned often of their sinful state, urged to make peace in time with the offended Deity while offered grace still invites them. For I will clear their darkened senses enough to soften their stony hearts, leading them to prayer, repentance, and proper obedience.

To prayer, repentance, and obedience, even if only attempted with sincere intent, my ear shall not be slow, nor my eye shut. I will place within them Conscience as a guide and judge. If they will listen to it, they shall gain light after light, well used. Persisting to the end, they shall safely arrive.

This long patience and day of grace -- those who neglect and scorn it shall never taste. Instead, the hard shall be hardened further, and the blind shall be blinded more, so that they stumble on and fall deeper. But only such as these do I exclude from mercy.

But all is not yet done. Man, by disobeying and breaking faith, sins against the highest authority of Heaven. By grasping at godhood, he loses everything. He has nothing left to pay for his treason except his own destruction and death. He and all his descendants must die -- either he dies, or justice must die -- unless someone else, able and willing, pays the full and rigid price: death for death.

Tell me, heavenly Powers, where shall we find such love? Which of you will become mortal to redeem Man's mortal crime and save the unjust through justice? Is there such dear charity in all of Heaven?" He asked, but all the heavenly choir stood silent. Silence filled Heaven. No one appeared to speak on Man's behalf, much less anyone who dared draw that deadly penalty onto his own head and set the ransom.

And now, without redemption, all of humanity would have been lost, condemned to Death and Hell by severe judgment, had not the Son of God, in whom the fullness of divine love dwelt, renewed his dearest plea.

"Father, your word has been given: Man shall find grace. And shall grace not find the means? Grace, the swiftest of your winged messengers, who visits all your creatures and comes to all unsought, uninvited, unexpected?

It is fortunate for Man that grace comes this way, for once dead in sins and lost, he can never seek her aid himself. He has no atonement or worthy offering to bring, being indebted and undone. So look at me: me for him, life for life, I offer. Let your anger fall on me.

Count me as Man. For his sake I will leave your embrace and this glory next to you, freely putting it aside, and at last die willingly for him. Let Death unleash all his fury on me. Under his gloomy power I shall not lie defeated for long. You have given me life in myself forever; through you I live.

Though I now yield to Death and become his due, all of me that can die -- yet once that debt is paid, you will not leave me in the loathsome grave as his prey. Nor will you allow my pure soul to dwell there forever in corruption.

But I shall rise victorious and defeat my conqueror, stripping him of his boasted prize. Death shall receive his own death-wound then and fall in disgrace, disarmed of his mortal sting. I shall lead Hell captive in triumph through the wide air, despite Hell's power, and display the forces of darkness bound in chains. You, seeing this from Heaven, shall look down and smile, while raised by you, I bring ruin to all my enemies.

Death itself, the last enemy, shall be destroyed. Its carcass shall glut the grave. Then, with the multitude of my redeemed, I shall enter Heaven, long absent, and return, Father, to see your face. No cloud of anger shall remain there, only assured peace and reconciliation. Wrath shall exist no more. In your presence there shall be complete and perfect joy."

His words ended, but his humble expression still spoke silently, breathing immortal love toward mortal humanity. Above all else shone his filial obedience, glad to be offered as a sacrifice. He awaited his great Father's will. Admiration and wonder seized all of Heaven at what this might mean and where it would lead. But soon the Almighty replied.

"O you who are the only peace found for humanity under wrath, both in Heaven and on Earth! O you, my sole delight! You know well how dear all my works are to me, and Man not least among them, though created last. For him I spare you from my heart and right hand, to save the whole lost race by losing you for a time.

Therefore, you whom you alone can redeem -- join their nature to your own nature. Become yourself a Man among men on Earth, made flesh when the time comes, of a virgin's seed, through wondrous birth. Be in Adam's place the head of all humanity, though you are Adam's son.

As all die in Adam, so in you, as from a second root, shall be restored as many as are restored -- without you, none. His crime makes all his descendants guilty. Your merit, applied to them, shall absolve all who renounce their own deeds, both the self-righteous and the unrighteous, and live in you, transplanted, receiving new life from you. So Man, as is most just, shall pay for Man -- being judged, dying, and rising again, raising his brothers with him, ransomed by his own precious life.
So heavenly love shall outdo hellish hate, giving to death and dying to redeem what hellish hate so easily destroyed and still destroys in those who refuse grace when it is offered.

Nor shall you, by descending to take on human nature, diminish or degrade your own divine nature. Because you have, though throned in highest bliss, equal to God and equally enjoying God-like fulfillment, given up everything to save a world from total loss, you have been found by merit more than by birthright to be the Son of God. You are found worthiest by being good, far more than by being great or high, because love has abounded in you more than glory abounds.

Therefore your humiliation shall exalt your human nature along with you to this throne. Here you shall sit as both God and Man, Son of both God and Man, anointed universal King. All power I give you. Reign forever and claim your earned reward. Under you as supreme Head, I place all Thrones, Principalities, Powers, and Dominions.

Every knee shall bow to you -- those in Heaven, those on Earth, and those under the Earth in Hell. When you, attended gloriously from Heaven, appear in the sky and send the summoning Archangels to proclaim your dread tribunal, all the living and all the dead of every past age shall hasten from every direction to the general judgment. Such a blast shall rouse them from their sleep.

Then, with all your saints assembled, you shall judge wicked men and angels. They shall be condemned and sink beneath your sentence. Hell, its numbers complete, shall then be shut forever. Meanwhile the world shall burn, and from its ashes shall spring new Heavens and a new Earth. There the just shall dwell and, after all their long trials, see golden days full of golden deeds, with joy, peace, and fair truth triumphant.

Then you shall lay aside your royal scepter, for it shall no longer be needed. God shall be all in all. But all you gods and heavenly beings, adore him who dies to bring all this to pass. Adore the Son and honor him as you honor me."

No sooner had the Almighty finished than all the multitude of angels raised a shout -- loud as from countless numbers, sweet as from blessed voices uttering joy. Heaven rang with jubilee and loud hosannas that filled the eternal regions. With solemn adoration, they bowed low toward both thrones and cast their crowns to the ground, crowns woven with amaranth and gold.

Immortal amaranth -- a flower that once bloomed in Paradise near the Tree of Life, but was soon removed to Heaven because of Man's sin. There it grows and blossoms, shading the fountain of life. The river of bliss rolls its amber stream through the middle of Heaven over Elysian flowers.

With these unfading flowers, the chosen spirits bound their shining hair, interwoven with beams of light. Now they tossed the loose garlands onto the bright pavement, which shone like a sea of jasper and smiled, colored with celestial roses.

Then, wearing their crowns again, they took up their golden harps -- harps always in tune, hanging glittering at their sides like quivers. With a sweet preamble of enchanting harmony, they began their sacred song and awakened sublime raptures.

No voice was absent, and every voice could join the melodious parts perfectly, such is the harmony of Heaven. First they sang of the Father -- Omnipotent, Unchangeable, Immortal, Infinite, Eternal King, the Author of all being, Fountain of light, himself invisible amid the glorious brightness where he sits enthroned, inaccessible. Even when he shades the full blaze of his beams behind a cloud drawn around him like a radiant shrine, his edges appear dark with excessive brightness. They still dazzle Heaven so that even the brightest Seraphim cannot approach but must veil their eyes with both wings.

Next they sang of the Son, begotten first of all creation, the Divine Image. In his clear countenance, without any cloud, the Almighty Father shines visibly, whom otherwise no creature can behold. The reflection of his glory remains impressed upon the Son, and his abundant Spirit rests upon him.

Through the Son, God created the Heaven of Heavens and all the Powers within them. Through the Son, he threw down the rebellious Dominions. On that day, the Son did not spare the Father's terrible thunder, nor did he stop his flaming chariot wheels that shook Heaven's everlasting frame while he drove over the necks of disarrayed, warring angels.

Returning from pursuit, the heavenly Powers acclaimed the Son alone, extolling him as the Son of the Father's might, sent to execute fierce vengeance on God's enemies. But not so upon Man. Though Man had fallen through the malice of those same rebels, the Father of mercy and grace did not judge Man so strictly, but was much more inclined to pity.

No sooner did the dear and only Son perceive that the Father was inclined to pity rather than strict judgment, than he offered himself to die for Man's sin, to reconcile the struggle between mercy and justice visible in the Father's face. Regardless of the bliss of sitting second only to God, he offered himself to die for humanity's offense. O unexampled love! Love nowhere to be found except in the Divine!

"Hail, Son of God, Savior of Men! Your name shall be the abundant subject of my song from now on, and my heart shall never forget your praise or separate it from your Father's praise." So they sang in Heaven above the starry sphere, spending their happy hours in joy and hymns.

Meanwhile, upon the firm, opaque globe of this round world, whose outer surface divides the luminous inner spheres from Chaos and the encroachment of ancient Darkness, Satan landed and walked about. From far off it had seemed a globe. Now it appeared a boundless continent -- dark, waste, and wild, under the frown of starless Night and the ever-threatening storms of Chaos blowing roughly around it under an unforgiving sky.

Except on the side facing the wall of Heaven, which though distant provided some faint reflection of less troubled, glimmering air, the Fiend walked freely in the spacious, desolate field. Like a vulture bred on the snowy ridges of the Himalayas, leaving a region scarce of prey to feast on the flesh of lambs or young goats on the hills where flocks graze, flying toward the springs of the Ganges or Indus --

But which first lands on the barren plains of Central Asia, where Chinese merchants drive their light cane wagons with sails before the wind -- so on this windy sea of land, the Fiend walked up and down alone, intent on his prey.

Alone, for no other creature, living or lifeless, could be found in this place. None yet, but in the future from the Earth, aerial vapors would fly up here -- all things transitory and vain. When sin had filled the works of humanity with vanity:

All vain things and all those who built their foolish hopes of glory or lasting fame or happiness in this life or the next; all who seek only the praise of others and find here fitting repayment, as empty as their deeds;
All Nature's malformed, monstrous, or mismatched works, dissolved on Earth, drift here, wandering in vain until the final dissolution -- not on the neighboring moon, as some have imagined.

The moon's silver fields more likely hold translated saints or middle spirits between the angelic and human kinds. To this place came those giants, born of ill-matched sons and daughters from the ancient world, with many a vain exploit, though renowned in their time.

The builders of Babel on the plain of Shinar came next, and still with vain ambition would build new Babels if they had the means. Others came individually: Empedocles, who leaped foolishly into Etna's flames to be thought a god, and Cleombrotus, who leaped into the sea to enjoy Plato's Elysium, and many more too numerous to name -- unformed souls, fools, hermits, and friars in white, black, and gray robes with all their trappings.

Here pilgrim wanderers roamed who had strayed so far to seek in Golgotha one who was dead, though he lives in Heaven. And those who, to be sure of Paradise, put on Dominican robes when dying, or in Franciscan garb thought to pass through in disguise.

They passed the seven planets, the fixed stars, the crystalline sphere that balances the wobble, and the primum mobile itself. Now Saint Peter seemed to wait for them at Heaven's gate with his keys. They lifted their feet at the base of Heaven's ascent, when suddenly a violent crosswind from either coast blew them sideways ten thousand leagues off course. Cowls, hoods, and habits with their wearers were tossed and torn to rags. Then relics, beads, indulgences, dispensations, pardons, and papal bulls -- all became sport for the winds. All these, whirled aloft, flew over the backside of the world, far off, into a broad Limbo, long afterward called the Paradise of Fools -- to few unknown.

Satan found all this as he passed over the dark globe, and long he wandered. At last a gleam of dawning light turned his hurried steps in that direction. Far off he could see a magnificent structure ascending by degrees up to the wall of Heaven.

At the top, far more richly adorned, appeared what looked like the gate of a kingly palace, with a frontispiece of diamond and gold embellished with thick, sparkling Eastern gems. The portal shone, impossible to replicate on Earth by any model or artist's brush.

These were stairs like those on which Jacob saw angels ascending and descending -- bright bands of guardians -- when he fled from Esau to Paddan-aram. In the field of Luz, dreaming by night under the open sky, he woke and cried: "This is the gate of Heaven!"

Each step held a mysterious meaning. The stairway did not always stand there but was sometimes drawn up into Heaven, invisible from below. Underneath it, a bright sea of jasper or liquid pearl flowed. Those who came from Earth, failing to arrive on their own, were carried over the lake on angels' wings, or flew across, transported in a chariot drawn by fiery horses.

The stairs were let down at this time, perhaps to tempt the Fiend with an easy ascent, or perhaps to make his exclusion from the doors of bliss more painful. Directly opposite, just above Paradise, there opened a passage down to Earth -- wide and accessible, wider by far than the one in later times over Mount Zion, though that one was large too, stretching over the Promised Land so dear to God.

Through this passage, God's angels frequently passed back and forth to visit the happy people below, carrying out the behests of Heaven. And his eye, with loving attention, watched over everything from Paneas, the source of the Jordan, to Beersheba, where the Holy Land borders Egypt and the Arabian shore.

The opening seemed as wide as the bounds set upon ocean waves. Satan, now on the lower stair, the one that scaled in golden steps toward Heaven's gate, looked down with wonder at the sudden view of all this world spread out at once before him. It was like when a scout, having traveled through dark and dangerous paths all night, at last reaches the crest of a high hill at cheerful dawn and unexpectedly discovers the fine prospect of some foreign land or renowned city with glittering spires and towers gilded by the rising sun.

Such wonder seized the malign Spirit, though he had already seen Heaven. But far more than wonder, envy seized him at the sight of this beautiful world. He surveyed it all around from his high position above the canopy of night's extended shadow, from the eastern point of Libra to the constellation that bears Andromeda far off beyond Atlantic seas. Then from pole to pole he viewed its breadth. Without further pause, he threw himself straight down into the world's first region, falling headlong and winding easily through the pure, clear air among innumerable stars. Distant they shone, but from nearby seemed like other worlds.

They seemed other worlds indeed, or happy islands like the legendary Hesperian gardens, fortunate fields, groves, and flowery valleys -- thrice-happy places. But who lived happily there, he did not stop to ask. Above them all, the golden sun, most like Heaven in splendor, drew his eye. Toward it he bent his course through the calm sky, though whether up or down, toward the center or away from it, was hard to say. There the great luminary, set apart from the common constellations that kept a respectful distance, dispensed its light far and wide. The other stars, as they moved in their dance computing days, months, and years, turned their various motions toward its warming lamp, turned by its magnetic beam. That beam gently warmed the whole universe, shooting invisible power deep into everything.

So wonderfully was the sun's station set. There the Fiend landed, on a spot such as perhaps no astronomer had ever seen through his telescope on the sun's bright surface. The place was bright beyond description compared to anything on Earth, whether metal or stone.

Not all alike, but all equally filled with radiant light, like glowing iron in a fire. If metal, part seemed gold and part silver. If stone, it was mostly carbuncle or chrysolite, ruby or topaz -- like the twelve jewels that shone in Aaron's breastplate, and another stone besides, more often imagined than actually seen: the Philosopher's Stone that alchemists had sought so long in vain, though they bound volatile Mercury and summoned old Proteus from the sea in various shapes, distilling him through their equipment to his original form.

No wonder then if fields and regions here breathed pure elixir and rivers ran with drinkable gold. The great alchemist Sun, though so far from us, produces with the earthly moisture mixed here in the dark so many precious things of glorious color and rare effect.

Here the Devil encountered new sights to gaze at, undazzled. His eyes commanded far and wide, for no obstacle of sight or shadow existed here -- nothing but pure sunshine, as when the sun's beams shine straight down at noon from the equator, casting no shadows. The air, clearer here than anywhere, sharpened his vision to see distant objects. He soon spotted, within range of sight, a glorious angel standing there -- the same one John saw in the sun.

The angel's back was turned, but his brightness was not hidden. A golden halo of sunny rays circled his head. His radiant hair, thick with wings, lay waving over his shoulders. He seemed to be employed on some important task, or else deep in thought.

The impure Spirit was glad, hoping now to find someone who could direct his wandering flight to Paradise, the happy home of Man -- his journey's end and the beginning of our sorrow. But first he chose to change his own appearance, which otherwise might cause him danger or delay.

Now he appeared as a young Cherub, not of the highest rank, yet with a face that smiled with celestial youth. Grace was suited to every limb, so well did he disguise himself. Under a small crown, his flowing hair played in curls on either cheek. He wore wings of many colors, sprinkled with gold.

His clothing was suited for speed, and he carried a silver wand before his modest steps. He did not approach unheard. The bright angel, warned by the sound, turned his radiant face. He was immediately recognized as the Archangel Uriel, one of the seven who stand nearest to God's throne in his presence, ready at command. They are his eyes, running through all the Heavens or down to Earth, carrying his swift errands over land and sea. Satan addressed him.

"Uriel, you who are first among those seven spirits that stand in sight of God's high throne, most gloriously bright, you are accustomed to interpret his great authentic will and bring it through highest Heaven, where all his sons await your embassy.

And here you are most likely, by supreme decree, similarly honored to frequently visit this new creation. An unspeakable desire to see and know all these wondrous works of his, but chiefly Man, his chief delight and favorite -- for whom he ordained all these wondrous works -- has brought me alone, wandering, from the choirs of Cherubim. Brightest Seraph, tell me: in which of all these shining spheres has Man his fixed home? Or has he none, but may choose to dwell in any of them?

Let me find him and, with secret awe or open admiration, behold him -- him on whom the great Creator has bestowed worlds and poured all these graces. So that in both him and all things, as is right, we may praise the universal Maker,

who has justly driven out his rebel enemies to the deepest Hell, and to repair that loss has created this new, happy race of men to serve him better. All his ways are wise." So spoke the false deceiver, undetected.

For neither Man nor Angel can detect hypocrisy, the only evil that walks invisibly, except to God alone, by his permissive will, through Heaven and Earth. Often, though wisdom keeps watch, suspicion sleeps at wisdom's gate, yielding its post to simplicity, while goodness suspects no ill where none appears. And now for once this fooled even Uriel, though he was regent of the Sun and known as the sharpest-sighted spirit in all Heaven.

In his own uprightness, Uriel returned this answer to the fraudulent impostor: "Fair Angel, your desire to know God's works and thereby glorify the great Master leads to nothing blameworthy but rather deserves praise. The more excessive it seems, the more it merits honor. It has led you here from your heavenly dwelling, alone, to witness with your own eyes what some, content with merely hearing about it, know only by report in Heaven.

For wonderful indeed are all his works, pleasant to know, and most worthy to be kept in memory with delight. But what created mind can comprehend their number, or the infinite wisdom that brought them forth yet hid their causes deep?

I was there when, at his word, the formless mass that was this world's raw material came together. Confusion heard his voice, and wild chaos stood ruled. Vast infinitude was confined. At his second command, darkness fled. Light shone, and order sprang from disorder.

Swiftly the heavy elements -- earth, water, air, and fire -- hurried to their appointed places. This ethereal fifth element of Heaven flew upward, spirited into various forms that rolled into spheres and became the countless stars you see, each moving as ordained.

Each star had its place and course assigned. The rest form the circuit wall of this universe. Look down at that globe -- its near side shines with reflected light from here. That place is Earth, the home of Man. That light is his day. Otherwise, as on the far side, night would reign. But the neighboring moon -- that bright star opposite -- provides timely help. With borrowed light, her three-phased face fills and empties each month, lighting the Earth and checking the darkness of night.

That spot I am pointing to is Paradise, Adam's home. Those tall, shady trees are his bower. You cannot miss the way. My own duties call me elsewhere." Having said this, he turned away. Satan, bowing low as is customary before higher spirits in Heaven, where no one neglects proper respect, took his leave. Toward the coast of Earth below, descending from the ecliptic, he threw himself in spiraling flight, dropping rapidly down until he landed on the top of Mount Niphates.

chapters.title: Book IV
paragraphs: Oh, if only that warning voice which John, who saw the Apocalypse, heard crying aloud in Heaven -- when the Dragon, defeated a second time, came down furious to take revenge on humanity: 'Woe to the inhabitants of the earth!' -- if only our first parents had been warned in time of their secret enemy's approach and escaped his deadly snare. For now Satan, newly inflamed with rage, came down as the tempter before becoming the accuser of humanity, to take out on innocent, fragile Man his loss of that first battle and his flight to Hell.

Yet not rejoicing in his speed, though bold from a distance and fearless, nor with any real cause to boast, he begins his terrible attempt. It boils and churns in his tumultuous breast, nearly ready to be born, and like a devilish weapon it recoils upon himself. Horror and doubt distract his troubled thoughts, stirring from the depths the Hell within him. For he carries Hell within himself and all around him. He cannot flee from Hell by changing his location, any more than he can flee from himself. Now conscience awakens the despair that had been sleeping, stirring the bitter memory of what he was, what he is, and what he must become -- still worse. From worse deeds, worse sufferings must follow.

Sometimes toward Eden, which now lay pleasantly in his view, he fixed his grieved, sad gaze. Sometimes he looked toward Heaven and the full-blazing sun, which now sat high at its noonday peak. Then, turning many thoughts over, he began with sighs.

"O you, crowned with surpassing glory, who look from your sole dominion like the God of this new world -- at whose sight all the stars hide their diminished heads -- to you I call, but with no friendly voice. I add your name, O Sun, only to tell you how I hate your beams. They remind me of what state I fell from and how glorious I once was, above even your sphere,
