until pride and worse ambition threw me down, warring in Heaven against Heaven's matchless King. Why did I do it? He deserved no such return from me. He created me in that bright eminence and never reproached anyone with his goodness. His service was not hard.

What less could I have done than offer him praise, the easiest repayment, and give him thanks? How richly deserved! Yet all his goodness only produced malice in me. Lifted so high, I scorned obedience and thought one step higher would make me the highest. I imagined I could in a moment cancel the immense debt of endless gratitude -- so burdensome, always paying yet always owing. I forgot what I still received from him. I did not understand that a grateful mind, by owing, does not truly owe but constantly pays, at once indebted and discharged. What burden is that? Oh, if his powerful destiny had ordained me some lower angel, I would have stood firm and been happy. No boundless hope would have raised my ambition! Yet why not? Some other Power equally great might have aspired and drawn me, though lowly, to his side. But other Powers equally great did not fall. They stand unshaken, armed against all temptations from within or without.

Did you have the same free will and power to stand? You did. Then whom or what can you accuse but Heaven's free love, dealt equally to all? Then let his love be cursed, since whether love or hate, it deals me eternal misery.

No -- cursed be you yourself, since your own will freely chose against his what it now so justly regrets. Miserable me! Which way shall I flee from infinite wrath and infinite despair? Every direction I flee is Hell. I myself am Hell.

And in the lowest depths, a still lower depth threatening to devour me opens wide. Compared to that, the Hell I now suffer seems like Heaven. Oh, then, relent at last. Is there no room left for repentance, none for pardon?

None except through submission. And that word my disdain forbids, along with my dread of shame among the spirits below me, whom I seduced with promises and boasts quite different from submission, bragging that I could overpower the Almighty. They have no idea how dearly I pay for that vain boast, under what torments I inwardly groan, while they worship me on the throne of Hell.

With crown and scepter raised high, I only fall lower, supreme in nothing but misery. Such is the joy that ambition finds. But suppose I could repent and could regain my former state by an act of grace -- how quickly would high position bring back high thoughts, how quickly would I take back what false submission had sworn? Comfort would cancel vows made in pain as forced and invalid.

For true reconciliation can never grow where wounds of deadly hatred have pierced so deep. It would only lead me to a worse relapse and a heavier fall. I would buy a brief reprieve at the price of double suffering.

My Punisher knows this. Therefore he is as far from granting peace as I am from begging for it. With all hope shut out, behold -- instead of us outcasts and exiles, his new delight: humanity created, and this world made for them.

So farewell, hope. And with hope, farewell fear. Farewell, remorse! All good is lost to me. Evil, be my good. Through evil I at least hold a divided empire with Heaven's King, and through evil I may perhaps reign over more than half,

as Man and this new world shall soon learn." While he spoke, each passion dimmed his face, which changed three times with paleness, fury, envy, and despair. These emotions marred his borrowed disguise and would have betrayed him as a counterfeit, if any eye had been watching.

For heavenly minds are always free from such foul disturbances. Becoming aware of this, he smoothed each perturbation with outward calm. He was the master craftsman of fraud, and the first to practice falsehood under a saintly appearance, concealing deep malice mixed with thoughts of revenge.

Yet he had not practiced enough to deceive Uriel once warned. Uriel's eye had followed him down the path he took. On the Assyrian mount, Uriel saw him disfigured far more than could happen to any spirit of a happy nature. He marked Satan's fierce gestures and maddened behavior when Satan thought himself alone, completely unobserved and unseen.

Satan traveled on and came to the border of Eden, where delightful Paradise, now closer, crowned with its green enclosure like a rural wall the flat top of a steep wilderness. The wilderness's shaggy sides were overgrown with thick, grotesque, wild undergrowth that denied all access. Overhead grew an insurmountable height of the loftiest shade -- cedar, pine, fir, and branching palm. It was a forest scene, and as the ranks ascended, shade above shade formed a stately wooded amphitheater. Yet higher still than the treetops, the green wall of Paradise rose up.

This wall gave our first father a broad view of the surrounding lowlands of his earthly domain. Higher than the wall stood a ring of the finest trees, loaded with the most beautiful fruit. Blossoms and fruit appeared at the same time, all golden, mixed with brightly enameled colors.

On these the sun impressed its beams more gladly than on any fair evening cloud or humid rainbow after God has showered the earth. So lovely the landscape seemed. And now air purer than pure met his approach, inspiring springlike delight and joy in the heart, strong enough to drive away all sadness except despair. Gentle breezes, fanning their fragrant wings, dispensed native perfumes and whispered of where they had stolen those sweet spoils. It was like when sailors who have rounded the Cape of Good Hope and passed Mozambique catch the northeast winds blowing Sabaean fragrances from the spice-rich shores of blessed Arabia. Well pleased, they slow their course, and for many a league old Ocean smiles, cheered by the welcome smell.

Those fragrant sweets entertained the Fiend just as well, though he came as their destroyer. He was even better pleased by them than Asmodeus was by the fishy fume that drove him, despite his infatuation, from the bride of Tobias's son, and sent him flying from Media to Egypt, where he was bound fast.

Now Satan had journeyed slowly and thoughtfully up the ascent of that steep, wild hill. But he found no further path, so thickly intertwined was the undergrowth of shrubs and tangling bushes, forming one continuous brake that blocked every trail for man or beast.

There was only one gate, and it faced east on the other side. When the arch-criminal saw this, he scorned to use the proper entrance. In contempt, with a single bound he leaped high over every barrier of hill or highest wall and landed clean on his feet inside. Like a prowling wolf driven by hunger to seek new hunting grounds, watching where shepherds pen their flocks at evening in fenced enclosures amid the secure field, who leaps easily over the fence into the fold --

or like a thief bent on stealing the fortune of some rich citizen, whose solid doors, cross-barred and bolted fast, fear no assault, who climbs in through the window or over the roof tiles -- so this first grand thief climbed into God's fold.

And so, ever since, corrupt hirelings have climbed into his church. From there Satan flew up and perched on the Tree of Life, the middle tree and tallest that grew there. He sat like a cormorant -- yet gained no true life from it. Instead he sat there plotting death for those who lived. He gave no thought to the virtue of that life-giving tree but used it only as a lookout point. What, properly used, would have been the pledge of immortality, he turned to the meanest purpose. So little does anyone but God alone know how to value the good that stands before them, instead perverting the best things to the worst abuse or the most trivial use.

Beneath him he now gazed with new wonder at Nature's entire wealth displayed in a compact space, appealing to every human sense -- indeed more than Nature's wealth, a Heaven on Earth. For blissful Paradise was God's garden, planted by him in the east of Eden. Eden stretched from Auran eastward to the royal towers of great Seleucia, built by Greek kings, or where the people of Eden had long before dwelt in Telassar. In this pleasant land, God created his far more pleasant garden.

From the fertile ground he caused all trees of the noblest kind to grow, delightful to see, smell, and taste. Among them all stood the Tree of Life, tall and prominent, blooming with heavenly fruit of golden plant-life. Next to the Tree of Life grew the Tree of Knowledge -- our death -- knowledge of good purchased dearly by knowing evil.

A large river flowed southward through Eden. It did not change its course but passed under the shaggy hill, swallowed underground. For God had raised that mountain as his garden's elevated plot upon the rapid current. Through veins of porous earth, the water was drawn up by natural thirst and rose as a fresh fountain. With many small streams it watered the garden. Then, reunited, it fell down the steep slope and met the lower river, which emerged from its dark underground passage and divided into four main streams. These wandered through many famous kingdoms and lands, which need not be described here.

It is better to tell, if words could do it justice, how from that sapphire fountain the rippling brooks rolled over oriental pearl and golden sand, wandering in delightful curves under hanging shade, running with nectar-like water, visiting each plant and feeding flowers worthy of Paradise. These flowers were not planted by fussy Art in beds and elaborate designs. Generous Nature poured them forth abundantly on hill, valley, and plain, both where the morning sun first warmly struck the open field and where unbroken shade darkened the noonday bowers. This place was a happy rural paradise of varied scenery.

Groves of rich trees wept fragrant gums and balm. Others bore fruit with burnished golden rind, hanging beautifully -- the legends of the Hesperides made real, if real anywhere. Between these stood lawns or level meadows with flocks grazing the tender grass, or palm-covered hillocks, or the flowery bosom of some well-watered valley spread with its treasure of flowers in every color, and roses without thorns.

On another side were shadowy grottoes and caves offering cool retreat, over which the vine spread its purple grapes and crept luxuriantly. Meanwhile murmuring waters fell down the sloping hills, either dispersing in separate streams or joining in a lake that, bordered by myrtle-crowned banks, held up its crystal mirror.

The birds formed their choir. Spring airs, breathing the fragrance of field and grove, tuned the trembling leaves, while universal Pan, joined with the Graces and the Hours in dance, led on eternal Spring. Not even the fair field of Enna, where Proserpine was gathering flowers when gloomy Dis carried her off -- herself a fairer flower -- which cost Ceres such grief searching through the world, could rival this Paradise. Nor could the sweet grove of Daphne by the Orontes and its inspired Castalian spring, nor the island of Nysa surrounded by the river Triton, where old Ham -- whom pagans called Ammon and Libyan Jove -- hid Amalthea and her beautiful son young Bacchus from his stepmother Rhea's eye.

Nor could Mount Amara, where Ethiopian kings guarded their children, though some believed it was the true Paradise under the equator near the Nile's source, enclosed with shining rock and a full day's journey high. That place was far removed from this garden in the Assyrian region, where the Fiend saw, without delight, everything delightful. He saw every kind of living creature, new and strange to his sight. Two among them were of far nobler form, erect and tall. Standing upright like gods, clothed in naked majesty with their natural dignity, they seemed lords of all.

And they deserved to seem so. In their faces shone the divine image of their glorious Maker -- truth, wisdom, holiness severe and pure (severe, but placed within true filial freedom, which is the source of genuine authority in human beings). Though the two were not equal, as their genders were not equal.

He was formed for thought and valor. She was formed for grace, softness, and sweet attractive charm. He was made for God alone, she for God through him. His fine, broad forehead and noble eyes declared absolute authority. Curling locks like hyacinth hung manfully from his parted hair, clustering but not reaching below his broad shoulders.

She wore her unadorned golden hair like a veil, loose and disheveled down to her slender waist, but waving in playful ringlets as the vine curls its tendrils. This implied her willing yielding to his gentle authority, given with modest pride and sweet, reluctant, loving hesitation.

Their intimate parts were not concealed then. There was no guilty shame, that dishonest shame about Nature's works, that dishonorable notion of honor. Sin-bred shame, how you have troubled all humanity with pretense, mere shows of seeming purity, and banished from human life its happiest condition: simplicity and spotless innocence!

So they walked on naked, not avoiding the sight of God or angel, for they knew no evil. Hand in hand they went, the loveliest pair that ever since have come together in love's embrace. Adam was the most handsome of all men who would ever be born from him, and Eve the fairest of all women who would descend from her.

Under a cluster of trees that stood whispering softly on a green spot by a fresh fountain, they sat down. After no more labor in their pleasant gardening than was needed to work up a healthy appetite and make rest more welcome, they turned to their supper of fruits. Delicious nectarine fruits the accommodating branches offered them as they reclined on the soft, flower-covered bank.

They chewed the savory pulp and, whenever they were thirsty, scooped the brimming stream from the rind. Gentle conversation, endearing smiles, and playful affection were not lacking, as befitted a beautiful couple joined in happy marriage, alone as they were. All around them, every beast of the earth played -- animals that have since gone wild and become the prey of forest hunts.

The lion romped and dandled a kid in its paw. Bears, tigers, lynxes, and leopards gamboled before them. The ungainly elephant, to amuse them, used all his strength and coiled his nimble trunk. Nearby, the sly serpent wove intricate Gordian knots with its braided length, giving unheeded proof of its fatal cunning. Other animals lay on the grass, some sitting contentedly after grazing, others chewing their cud before sleep. For the sun, now declining, was hastening toward the ocean islands, and in the ascending sky the stars that herald evening were rising.

Satan, still staring from where he first stood, barely managed to recover his faltering voice and sadly spoke: "O Hell! What do my eyes behold with grief! Into our former place of bliss, creatures of a different kind are advanced so high -- earthborn perhaps, not spirits, yet scarcely inferior to the brightest heavenly spirits. My thoughts follow them with wonder. I could even love them, so vividly does the divine likeness shine in them, and such grace the hand that formed them has poured upon their shapes.

"Ah, gentle pair! You have no idea how near your transformation is. All these delights will vanish and deliver you to misery -- all the worse because your present taste of joy is so sweet. Happy, but too ill-protected to remain happy long. This high paradise, your little Heaven, is poorly defended to keep out a foe such as has now entered. Yet I am no deliberate enemy to you, whom I could even pity in your approaching doom, though no one pities me. I seek alliance with you, and a bond so tight that I must live with you, or you with me, from now on. My dwelling may not please your senses the way this fair Paradise does, yet accept what your Maker's work provides. He gave it to me, and I give it just as freely. Hell shall open its widest gates to welcome you both, and send forth all its kings. There will be plenty of room, unlike these narrow limits, to receive your numerous offspring. If no better place can be found, blame him who reluctantly forces me to take revenge on you, who have done me no wrong, for the sake of him who wronged me.

And even if I should melt at your harmless innocence, as indeed I do, still public duty, honor, and the expansion of my empire through revenge by conquering this new world compels me now to do what otherwise, damned as I am, I would loathe to do."

So spoke the Fiend, excusing his devilish deeds with necessity -- the tyrant's constant plea. Then from his high perch on that tall tree, he descended among the playful herd of four-footed creatures. He took on first one animal's form, then another, as their shapes best served his purpose, drawing nearer to observe his prey. Undetected, he hoped to learn more about their condition from what they said or did. Now he stalked around them like a lion with a fiery glare.

Then like a tiger who has spotted two gentle fawns at play in some clearing, he crouched low, then rose and shifted position repeatedly, choosing his ground, ready to rush and seize them both, one in each paw. Just then, Adam, first of men, turned to Eve, first of women, and began to speak. This made Satan all ears, eager to hear what they would say.

"Sole partner and sole sharer of all these joys, dearer to me than all of them -- the Power that made us, and made this ample world for us, must surely be infinitely good, and as generous and free with his goodness as he is infinite.

He raised us from the dust and placed us here in all this happiness, though we have earned nothing from his hand and can do nothing he needs. He asks from us no other service than to keep this one easy rule: of all the trees in Paradise that bear such delicious and varied fruit, we are not to taste the one Tree of Knowledge, planted beside the Tree of Life.

So close does death grow to life, whatever death is -- some dreadful thing, no doubt. For you know well that God has declared it means death to taste that tree. It is the only sign of our obedience remaining, among so many signs of power, rule, and dominion given to us over all other creatures that possess earth, air, and sea. Let us not resent one easy prohibition, when we enjoy such unlimited freedom in everything else, and such boundless choice of countless delights.

Let us always praise him and celebrate his generosity, following our pleasant task of pruning these growing plants and tending these flowers. Even if it were hard work, it would still be sweet with you." To this Eve replied: "O you for whom and from whom I was formed, flesh of your flesh, without whom I have no purpose, my guide and head -- what you have said is just and right.

For we owe him all our praises and daily thanks. I especially, since I enjoy by far the happier lot in enjoying you, who surpass me by so great a degree, while you can find no companion equal to yourself.

I often remember that day when I first woke from sleep and found myself lying under a shade on flowers, wondering greatly where and what I was, how I got there, and how. Not far away, a murmuring sound of water came from a cave and spread into a still, clear pool, as pure as the sky above. I went there with inexperienced thoughts and lay down on the green bank to gaze into the smooth, clear lake, which seemed to me like another sky.

As I bent down to look, a shape appeared directly opposite in the watery gleam, bending to look at me. I pulled back startled. It pulled back too. But pleased, I soon returned, and pleased, it returned just as quickly with answering looks of sympathy and love. I would have fixed my eyes there forever, pining with vain desire, had not a voice warned me: 'What you see there, fair creature, is yourself.'

'It comes and goes with you. But follow me, and I will bring you to where no mere reflection awaits your coming and your soft embrace -- he whose image you are. You shall enjoy him inseparably as your own. You shall bear multitudes like yourself and be called Mother of the human race.' What could I do but follow immediately, led by that invisible guide?

Until I spotted you, fair indeed and tall, under a plane tree. Yet you seemed to me less fair, less winningly gentle, less lovably mild than that smooth watery reflection. I turned back. You followed, crying aloud: 'Return, fair Eve!

'From whom do you flee? You are part of him you flee from -- his flesh, his bone. To give you life, I lent from my side, nearest my heart, substantial being, so that you might be forever by my side as my dear, individual comfort.'

'Part of my soul, I seek you and claim you as my other half.' With that, your gentle hand seized mine. I yielded. And from that moment I have seen how beauty is surpassed by manly grace and wisdom, which alone is truly fair."

So spoke our universal mother, and with eyes of innocent conjugal attraction and gentle surrender, she half-embraced and leaned upon our first father. Half her swelling breast met his, bare beneath the flowing gold of her loose hair. He, delighted both by her beauty and her loving devotion, smiled down at her with superior love, as Jupiter smiles on Juno when he fills the clouds with rain that brings May flowers. He pressed her lips with pure kisses. The Devil turned aside in envy, yet with malicious jealousy eyed them sideways and complained to himself.

"Hateful sight! Tormenting sight! These two, paradised in one another's arms -- a happier Eden in themselves -- shall have their fill of bliss upon bliss, while I am thrust into Hell, where neither joy nor love exists. Among our other torments, not the least, fierce desire burns forever unfulfilled, longing in pain.

Yet let me not forget what I have learned from their own mouths. Not everything is theirs, it seems. One fatal tree stands there, called the Tree of Knowledge, forbidden to them. Knowledge forbidden? How suspicious, how unreasonable! Why should their Lord begrudge them that? Can it be a sin to know?

Can it mean death? Do they remain upright only through ignorance? Is that their happy state -- the proof of their obedience and faith? What a fine foundation on which to build their ruin! I will stir up in them a greater desire to know and to reject envious commands invented to keep them low, when knowledge might raise them equal with the gods. Aspiring to become like gods, they will taste the fruit and die. What else could follow? But first I must carefully search this garden and leave no corner unexplored.

Perhaps I will come across some wandering spirit of Heaven by a fountain or in a thick shade, from whom I can learn more. Live while you may, happy pair. Enjoy your short pleasures, for long sorrows are coming to replace them!"

So saying, he scornfully turned his proud steps, but with sly caution began to roam through wood, wasteland, hill, and valley. Meanwhile, at the farthest point of the horizon where Heaven meets earth and ocean, the setting sun slowly descended. Its evening rays shone directly against the eastern gate of Paradise, level with a rock of alabaster that piled up to the clouds, clearly visible from far away, winding upward with a single accessible path from the earth to one high entrance.

The rest was craggy cliff that overhung as it rose, impossible to climb. Between these rocky pillars sat Gabriel, chief of the angelic guards, waiting for night. Around him the unarmed youth of Heaven exercised in heroic games. Close at hand stood celestial armor -- shields, helmets, and spears hung high, flashing with diamond and gleaming with gold.

Uriel came gliding there on a sunbeam, swift as a shooting star that cuts across the autumn night when burning vapors streak the air, showing the mariner which direction to watch for dangerous winds. He began urgently.

"Gabriel, by lot your assignment includes the charge and strict watch over this happy place, to ensure no evil thing approaches or enters. Today at high noon, a spirit came to my sphere who seemed zealous to learn more about the Almighty's works, especially Man, God's latest creation made in his own image. I observed his course, directed entirely toward speed, and noted his airy movement.

But on the mount north of Eden, where he first landed, I detected that his expression was alien to Heaven, darkened with foul passions. My eye continued to follow him, but I lost sight of him in the shadows. I fear one of the banished crew has ventured up from the Deep to cause new trouble. Your task is to find him."

The winged warrior replied: "Uriel, no wonder your perfect sight, from the bright center of the sun where you are stationed, sees far and wide. Through this gate, no one passes under my watch except those well known from Heaven. Since noon, no creature has come through. If some spirit of another kind has deliberately leaped over these earthly boundaries, you know how hard it is to keep out a spiritual being with physical barriers.

But if he lurks within these grounds, in whatever shape, I shall know by morning." So he promised. Uriel returned to his post on that bright beam, which now carried him sloping downward to the sun as it sank beneath the Azores -- whether the mighty sun itself had rolled that far in its daily course, or this lesser-known revolving Earth, by shorter flight eastward, had left him there, painting the western clouds with reflected purple and gold.

Now still evening came on. Twilight gray had dressed everything in her sober uniform. Silence accompanied it. Beasts and birds settled into their grassy beds and nests, all except the wakeful nightingale.

She sang her amorous song all night long. Silence was pleased to listen. Now the sky glowed with living sapphires. Hesperus, who led the starry host, rode brightest until the moon, rising in clouded majesty, at last unveiled her peerless light as apparent queen and threw her silver mantle over the darkness.

Then Adam spoke to Eve: "Fair companion, the hour of night and the quiet of all things remind us of the rest we need. God has established labor and rest for us in succession, like day and night. The timely dew of sleep, now falling with soft, drowsy weight, closes our eyelids. Other creatures roam idle all day long, unemployed, and need less rest.

Man has his daily work of body or mind appointed to him, which declares his dignity and shows Heaven's regard for all his ways. Other animals range about without purpose, and God takes no account of their activities.

Tomorrow, before fresh morning light streaks the east, we must rise and return to our pleasant work. We need to tend those flowering arbors, those green pathways, our noonday walks where branches have grown so thick they mock our limited gardening and need more hands than ours to trim their wild growth.

Those fallen blossoms too, and those dripping resins that lie scattered, unsightly and rough, need clearing if we want to walk comfortably. Meanwhile, as Nature wills, night tells us to rest." To this Eve, adorned with perfect beauty, replied: "My creator and commander, what you bid I obey without argument, for God ordains it so.

God is your law, and you are mine. To know nothing more is woman's happiest wisdom and her praise. Talking with you, I forget all time. Every season and every change pleases me alike. Sweet is the breath of morning with its rising charm and the earliest birds singing. Pleasant is the sun when it first spreads its eastern beams on herb, tree, fruit, and flower, glistening with dew. Fragrant is the fertile earth after soft showers. Sweet is the coming of mild evening, then silent night with this her solemn nightingale, this fair moon, and these gems of Heaven, her starry train.

But neither morning's breath with the charm of earliest birds, nor the rising sun on this delightful land, nor herb, fruit, or flower glistening with dew, nor fragrance after showers, nor grateful mild evening, nor silent night, nor a walk by moonlight or glittering starlight -- none of these is sweet without you.

But why do these lights shine all night long? For whom is this glorious display, when sleep has shut everyone's eyes?" Our first ancestor replied: "Daughter of God and Man, accomplished Eve, these stars have their course to complete around the earth by tomorrow evening, and in order, though to nations yet unborn, they set and rise, preparing ministering light.

This prevents total darkness from reclaiming its old dominion at night and extinguishing life in Nature and all things. These gentle fires not only give light but with their warmth nurture, temper, and sustain all kinds of growth on Earth, making them more receptive to the Sun's more potent rays.

So these lights, though unseen in the depths of night, do not shine in vain. Do not think that, even if humans did not exist, Heaven would lack spectators or God would lack praise. Millions of spiritual beings walk the Earth unseen, both when we are awake and when we sleep.

All of them ceaselessly praise his works both day and night. How often from the steep slope of some echoing hill or thicket have we heard celestial voices singing to the midnight air, either alone or answering one another's notes, singing of their great Creator? Often in bands while keeping watch or making their nightly rounds, with heavenly instrumental music joined in full harmony, their songs divide the night and lift our thoughts to Heaven."

Talking this way, hand in hand, they walked alone to their blissful bower. It was a place chosen by the sovereign Gardener when he designed everything for Man's delight. The roof was woven with the thickest cover of shade -- laurel, myrtle, and whatever grew higher with firm, fragrant leaves. On either side, acanthus and fragrant bushes fenced up a green wall. Beautiful flowers -- irises of every hue, roses, and jasmine -- reared their bright heads between and created a mosaic pattern. Underfoot, violets, crocuses, and hyacinths formed a rich carpet, more colorful than the costliest inlaid stone. No other creature -- bird, beast, insect, or worm -- dared enter, such was their awe of Man. No sacred and secluded bower, even those imagined for Pan, Sylvanus, or woodland Nymph or Faunus, was ever as beautiful. Here, in this private retreat, with flowers, garlands, and sweet herbs, Eve adorned her first bridal bed.

Heavenly choirs sang the wedding hymn on the day when the guardian angel brought her to Adam in naked beauty more adorned and more lovely than Pandora, whom the gods endowed with all their gifts -- and, alas, too similar in sad outcome. For when Hermes brought Pandora to the foolish son of Japetus, she ensnared mankind with her fair looks, as revenge for the theft of Jove's sacred fire.

So, arriving at their shady lodge, both stood and turned and worshiped under the open sky the God who made both sky, air, earth, and heaven -- all that they could see: the moon's radiant globe and the starry sky. "You also made the night, almighty Maker, and you made the day. We have finished the work you assigned to us, happy in our mutual help and mutual love, the crown of all our joy, ordained by you. This delightful place is too large for just the two of us. Your abundance goes ungathered and falls to the ground.

But you have promised from us two a race to fill the Earth, who shall join us in praising your infinite goodness, both when we wake and when, as now, we seek your gift of sleep." Having said this together in unison, and performing no other rites but the pure worship God loves best, they entered their innermost bower hand in hand. Relieved of having removed the troublesome coverings that we wear, they lay straight down side by side. Adam did not turn from his fair wife, I believe, nor did Eve refuse the sacred rites of married love.

Whatever austere moralists say about purity, innocence, and proper conduct, slandering as impure what God declares pure and commands to some while leaving it free to all -- our Maker commands us to increase. Who commands us to abstain? Only our destroyer, the enemy of God and Man.

Hail, married Love, mysterious law and true source of human offspring! The sole private possession in a Paradise where everything else is shared! Through you, lustful adultery was driven from human society to range among the beasts. Through you, founded in reason, loyal, just, and pure, the dear bonds of father, son, and brother were first established.

Far be it from me to call you sinful or blameworthy, or to think you unfit for the holiest place -- you, the perpetual fountain of domestic happiness, whose bed is undefiled and declared pure, both now and as the saints and patriarchs of old practiced it.

Here Love employs his golden arrows, here lights his constant lamp and waves his purple wings. Here he reigns and celebrates -- not in the bought smiles of loveless, joyless, passionless prostitution, nor in the courtly flirtations, mixed dances, wanton masquerades, or midnight balls, nor in the serenades that the starving lover sings to his proud, scornful beauty, best answered with disdain.

These two, lulled by the nightingale, slept embracing. On their naked limbs the flowered canopy showered roses, which morning would restore. Sleep on, blessed pair! And oh, remain happiest of all, if you seek no happier state and know enough to know no more.

Night had now measured half its shadowy course up the vast dome beneath the heavens. From their ivory station, the Cherubim issued forth at the usual hour and stood armed for their night watch in military formation.

Gabriel spoke to his second-in-command: "Uzziel, take half our forces and patrol the south with the strictest watch. The rest will circle the north. Our routes will meet at the western point." They divided like flames -- half wheeling left, half wheeling right.

From among them Gabriel called two strong and skilled spirits who stood near him and gave them this assignment: "Ithuriel and Zephon, fly with speed and search through this garden. Leave no corner unchecked. But focus especially on where those two fair creatures are lodging, now probably asleep and unguarded.

This evening, arriving from the direction of the setting sun, Uriel reports that an infernal spirit has been seen heading this way -- escaped from the bars of Hell, who would have thought it! -- and no doubt bent on some wicked errand. Wherever you find such a being, seize it immediately and bring it here."

With these orders, Gabriel led his shining troops onward, dazzling the moon. Ithuriel and Zephon headed straight for the bower in search of the one they sought. There they found him, crouching like a toad close to Eve's ear. With his devilish skill, he was trying to reach the organs of her imagination to forge illusions, phantasms, and dreams.

Or perhaps, by injecting venom, he hoped to corrupt the animal spirits that rise from pure blood like gentle breaths from clear rivers, and so raise at least disturbing, discontented thoughts -- vain hopes, vain aims, and uncontrolled desires inflated with arrogant ideas that breed pride.

While he was intent on this, Ithuriel lightly touched him with his spear. For no falsehood can endure the touch of celestial power but is forced back into its true form. Satan started up, revealed and caught by surprise. It was like when a spark lands on a heap of gunpowder stored in a magazine against a rumored war -- the dark grain suddenly blazes and sets the air on fire.

Just so suddenly Satan sprang up in his own terrible form. The two fair angels stepped back, half amazed at the sudden sight of the grisly king. Yet unmoved by fear, they confronted him: "Which of those rebel spirits condemned to Hell have you come from, escaped from your prison? And why, transformed, were you sitting like an enemy in ambush, watching over these sleepers?"

"Don't you know me?" said Satan, filled with scorn. "You knew me once as no mere equal for you, sitting where you dared not fly. Not to recognize me shows your own insignificance, the lowest of your company. Or if you do know me, why bother asking, and why begin your message with unnecessary questions that will end as uselessly?"

Zephon answered his scorn with scorn: "Do not imagine, fallen spirit, that your form is the same or your brightness undiminished, as when you stood upright and pure in Heaven. That glory departed from you when you ceased to be good. You now resemble your sin and your dark, foul place of punishment.

But come, for you will certainly answer to the one who sent us, whose job is to keep this place inviolate and protect these inhabitants from harm." So spoke the Cherub. His grave rebuke, severe yet graced with youthful beauty, carried an invincible authority. The Devil stood abashed. He felt how powerful genuine goodness is and saw how lovely virtue appears. He saw and mourned his loss. But most of all, he was stung to discover his own brightness visibly diminished. Yet he seemed undaunted: "If I must fight, let it be with the best -- the commander, not the messenger -- or all at once. More glory will be won, or less lost." Zephon boldly replied: "Your fear will spare us the trouble of testing what even the least of us can do single-handedly against you, wicked and therefore weak."

The Fiend made no reply, overcome with rage. Like a proud horse reined in, he went haughtily forward, champing at the bit. He considered it pointless to fight or flee. A divine authority from above had subdued his heart, though nothing else could have intimidated him. Now they drew near the western point where the two half-patrols met and stood in joined formation, awaiting their next order. Gabriel, their chief, called out from the front.

"Friends! I hear nimble feet hurrying this way. By their glimmering shapes I can make out Ithuriel and Zephon through the darkness. With them comes a third of royal bearing but faded splendor. By his walk and fierce manner, he seems to be the Prince of Hell himself. He is not likely to leave without a fight.

Stand firm, for defiance glares in his face." He had barely finished when the two arrived and briefly reported whom they had brought, where they found him, how he was occupied, and what form he had taken. Gabriel addressed the prisoner sternly.

"Why have you, Satan, broken the bounds set on your transgressions and disturbed the duties of others who do not approve of breaking God's laws by your example, but have every right to question your bold intrusion into this place,

where you seem employed to violate the sleep of those whose dwelling God has planted here in happiness?" Satan replied with a contemptuous expression: "Gabriel, you had the reputation of being wise in Heaven, and I thought so too. But this question makes me doubt it. Is there anyone who loves his own suffering?

Who would not, finding the way, break free from Hell, though sentenced to stay there? You would do the same, without question, and boldly go to whatever place was farthest from pain, where you might hope to exchange torment for comfort and grief for delight. That is what I came here seeking.

This should make sense even to you, who know only good and have never experienced evil. Will you invoke the will of him who confines us? Let him make the iron gates of that dark prison more secure, if he really intends us to stay there. That answers your question.

The rest is true: they found me where they say. But that does not imply violence or harm." The warlike angel moved forward, half-smiling with disdain, and replied: "What a loss to Heaven of one who could judge wisely, now that Satan has fallen! Folly overthrew him, and now he returns from his escaped prison, gravely debating whether to consider wise or foolish those who ask what boldness brought him here unlicensed from his prescribed bounds in Hell.

So wise he judges it to flee from punishment! Keep judging that way, presumptuous one, until the wrath you bring upon yourself by fleeing meets your flight sevenfold increased, and scourges that wisdom back to Hell -- wisdom that has not yet taught you anything better than that no pain can equal the anger of an infinite power provoked.

But why did you come alone? Why did not all of Hell break loose with you? Is the pain less for them, less worth fleeing from? Or are they braver than you at enduring it? Courageous Chief -- the first to flee from suffering! If you had given this reason for your flight to the army you deserted, you would surely not have come as a lone fugitive."

The Fiend answered with a stern frown: "Not because I endure less than others, or shrink from pain, insulting angel! You know well I withstood your fiercest attack, when volleys of devastating thunder came to your aid and backed your otherwise undaunting spear.
But your words, as before, show your inexperience in what is required of a faithful leader after hard trials and past failures: not to risk everything through dangers he has not first tested himself.

Therefore I alone first undertook to cross the desolate abyss and scout this newly created world, which was rumored in Hell. I came hoping to find a better dwelling and to settle my afflicted forces here on Earth or in the air between,

though we may have to fight once more for possession against you and your comfortable legions, whose easier duty is to serve your Lord high in Heaven with hymns, practicing bowing and cringing rather than fighting." The warrior angel quickly replied.

"First you claim it was wise to flee from pain, then you say you came as a spy. This argues not a leader but a proven liar. Satan -- could you faithfully add that word? O sacred name of faithfulness, profaned!

Faithful to whom? To your mutinous crew? An army of fiends -- a fitting body for such a head! Was this the discipline and loyalty you pledged? Your military obedience, to dissolve allegiance to the acknowledged supreme Power?

And you, sly hypocrite, who now would pose as a champion of liberty -- you who more than anyone once fawned, cringed, and slavishly worshiped Heaven's majestic Monarch! Why? Only in the hope of deposing him and ruling in his place.

But hear my warning. Go back to where you fled from! If from this hour you appear within these sacred boundaries, I will drag you back in chains to the infernal pit and seal you there so securely that you will never again scorn the easily passed gates of Hell."

So Gabriel threatened. But Satan, giving no heed to threats, grew even more enraged and replied: "Talk of chains when I am actually your captive, proud boundary-guarding Cherub! But before then, expect to feel a far heavier burden from my prevailing arm, even though Heaven's King rides on your wings while you and your fellow servants, accustomed to the yoke, pull his triumphal chariot in procession through the star-paved road of Heaven."

While he spoke, the angelic squadron glowed fiery red. Sharpening their ranks into crescent formations, they began to close around him with leveled spears, thick as a field of ripe grain that waves and bends in the wind, while the anxious farmer worries his harvest may prove worthless chaff. On the other side, Satan, alarmed, collected all his might and stood expanded like Tenerife or Atlas, immovable.

His stature reached the sky. Horror sat plumed on his crest. In his grasp he held what seemed both spear and shield. Terrible deeds might have followed -- not just Paradise but perhaps the starry vault of Heaven itself, or at least all the elements, would have been torn apart by the violence of this conflict, had not the Eternal, to prevent such horrific battle, hung forth in Heaven his golden scales. These are still seen between the constellations of Virgo and Scorpio. In them he first weighed all created things -- the round Earth balanced against the surrounding air. Now he weighed the outcomes of their potential conflict, putting two weights in the scales: one for parting, one for fighting.

The weight for fighting flew quickly upward and kicked the beam -- showing it was the lighter, less favored outcome. Gabriel, noticing this, spoke to the Fiend: "Satan, I know your strength, and you know mine. Neither is our own but given. What folly then to boast about what weapons can do, since your power extends no further than Heaven permits, and mine, though now doubled enough to trample you like dirt? For proof, look up and read your fate written in that celestial sign,

where you are weighed and shown how light and weak you are, if you resist." The Fiend looked up and recognized his own side of the scale rising high in the air, outweighed. Without another word, he fled, murmuring. And with him fled the shadows of night.

chapters.title: Book V
paragraphs: Now Morning, advancing her rosy steps in the eastern sky, sowed the earth with orient pearl. Adam woke as usual, for his sleep was light and airy, bred from pure digestion and mild vapors, dispersed by nothing more than the sound of leaves and murmuring streams -- Aurora's fan -- and the bright morning song of birds on every branch. His wonder was all the greater, then, to find Eve still unwakened beside him, her hair in disarray and her cheeks flushed, as though from troubled rest. Leaning half-raised on his side, he gazed at her with looks of tender love, admiring her beauty, which whether waking or sleeping, radiated its own special graces.

Then with a voice as mild as when the west wind breathes upon flowers, softly touching her hand, he whispered: "Awake, my fairest, my bride, my latest discovery, Heaven's last and best gift, my ever-new delight!

Awake! The morning shines and the fresh field calls us. We are missing the best time to see how our young plants are sprouting, how the citrus grove is blooming, what the myrrh and balsam are producing, how Nature paints her colors, and how the bee sits on each bloom extracting liquid sweetness." Such whispering woke her, but with a startled look she turned to Adam and, embracing him, spoke: "O you in whom my thoughts find all their rest, my glory, my perfection! I am glad to see your face and the returned morning. For this night -- such a night as I have never passed before -- I have dreamed, if it was a dream, not as I usually do of you and the day's work past or tomorrow's plans, but of offense and trouble, which my mind never knew until this disturbing night.

I dreamed that close to my ear someone called me to walk in a gentle voice. I thought it was yours. It said: 'Why do you sleep, Eve? Now is the pleasant time, the cool and silent hour, except where silence yields to the nightingale who now sings his sweetest love-song.
The full moon reigns with a more pleasing light, setting off the face of things with shadow. All this beauty is wasted if no one sees it. Heaven wakes with all its eyes.
Whom should they behold but you, Nature's desire, in whose sight all things rejoice, drawn by your beauty to gaze in rapture?' I rose as if at your call but could not find you.
I walked on, and it seemed I walked alone through paths that brought me suddenly to the forbidden Tree of Knowledge. It seemed much fairer to my imagination than by day.

As I gazed in wonder, beside it stood one shaped and winged like the angels we have often seen. His dewy hair dripped ambrosia. He too gazed at the tree and said: 'O fair tree, loaded with fruit! Does no one deign to ease your burden and taste your sweetness? Neither God nor Man? Is knowledge so despised? 'Or what jealousy or prohibition forbids the taste? Whoever forbids it, no one shall keep me from your offered bounty any longer. Why else were you placed here?' Without hesitating, he boldly reached out, plucked the fruit, and tasted it. A cold horror chilled me at such daring words backed by such a daring deed.

But he, overjoyed, said: 'O divine fruit, sweet in yourself, but much sweeter picked this way -- forbidden here, it seems, as fit only for gods, yet able to make gods of men! And why not gods of men, since good grows more abundant the more it is shared, honoring the author rather than diminishing him? 'Here, happy creature, fair angelic Eve! Share it too. Happy as you are, you can be happier still.
You cannot be more worthy than you are, but taste this and henceforth be counted among the gods -- not confined to Earth but sometimes ascending to Heaven like us, by your own merit.
See what life the gods live there, and live that life yourself!' So saying, he drew near and held the fruit to my very mouth -- the same fruit he had plucked.

Its pleasant, savory smell so quickened my appetite that I felt I could not help but taste it. At once I flew up to the clouds with him, and beneath us I saw the immense Earth stretched out in a wide, varied prospect.
I wondered at my flight and transformation to this high elevation. Then suddenly my guide was gone. I felt myself sink and fall asleep. But oh, how glad I was to wake and find it was only a dream!"

Thus Eve related her night's experience, and Adam answered sadly. "Best image of myself, dearer half -- the trouble that disturbed your thoughts tonight concerns me equally. I cannot like this strange dream. I fear it springs from some evil source. Yet how could evil find harbor in you, who were created pure? But know that in the soul there are many lesser faculties that serve Reason as their chief. Among these, Imagination holds the next office. From all external things that the five watchful senses present to it, Imagination forms images and airy shapes.
Reason then joins or separates these, forming all that we affirm or deny -- what we call knowledge or opinion. Then Reason retires to its private chamber when nature rests.
Often in Reason's absence, unruly Imagination wakes to imitate her but, misjoining shapes, produces wild work -- especially in dreams -- mismatching words and deeds from the past or recent events.
I think I can find some resemblances to our talk last evening in your dream, but with strange additions. Yet do not be troubled.

Evil may enter the mind of God or Man and pass through without being approved, leaving no stain or blame behind. This gives me hope that what you dreamed with horror in your sleep, you will never consent to do while awake.

So do not be discouraged. Do not cloud those looks that are usually more cheerful and serene than when the fair morning first smiles on the world. Let us go to our fresh work among the groves, fountains, and flowers that now open their sweetest scents, saved from the night and stored for you."
So he cheered his fair wife, and she was cheered. But silently she let fall a gentle tear from each eye and wiped them with her hair.

Two other precious drops that stood ready, each in their crystal channel, he kissed away before they fell, seeing them as gracious signs of sweet remorse and loving reverence afraid of having offended.
So all was resolved, and they hurried to the field.

But first, as soon as they came out from under their shady arbored roof into the open daylight, with the sun barely risen, his dewy rays shooting parallel to the earth, revealing the wide landscape of Paradise and Eden's happy plains to the east, they bowed low in worship and began their morning prayers, paid faithfully each day in varied expression.

They lacked neither varied style nor holy rapture to praise their Maker in fitting words, spoken or sung spontaneously. Such ready eloquence flowed from their lips, in prose or measured verse, more tuneful than any lute or harp could enhance. And so they began. "These are your glorious works, Parent of Good, Almighty! This wondrous and beautiful universal frame is yours. How much more wondrous, then, must you be! Unspeakable, you who sit above these heavens, invisible to us or only dimly seen in these, your lowest works.
Yet even these declare your goodness beyond thought and your divine power. Speak, you who can best tell -- you sons of light, you angels!

For you behold him and with songs and harmonies circle his throne rejoicing, day without night. You in Heaven, and all you creatures on Earth, join together to praise him, first, last, midst, and without end. Fairest of stars, last in night's train -- or if you belong instead to the dawn, sure pledge of day, crowning the smiling morning with your bright circle -- praise him in your sphere while day arises in that sweet first hour.

You, Sun, both the eye and soul of this great world, acknowledge him as your greater. Sound his praise in your eternal course, both when you climb and when you reach high noon and when you set. Moon, that now meets the eastern sun and now flies away with the fixed stars on that sphere that moves --  and you five other wandering lights that move in mystical dance, not without song -- sound his praise, he who called light out of darkness.

Air, and you elements, the eldest birth of Nature's womb, that run in perpetual cycles, constantly mixing and nourishing all things -- let your ceaseless changes give our great Maker still new praise.

You mists and vapors that now rise from hill or steaming lake, gray or dusky, until the sun paints your fleecy edges with gold -- rise in honor of the world's great Author. Whether you deck the sky with clouds or water the thirsty earth with falling showers, rising or falling, advance his praise. His praise, you winds that blow from four directions, breathe soft or loud.

Wave your tops in worship, you pines, with every plant, in a sign of devotion. Fountains, and you streams that warble as you flow, tune your melodious murmurs to his praise. Join voices, all you living souls. You birds that sing as you ascend toward the gate of Heaven, carry his praise on your wings and in your notes. You that glide through waters, and you that walk the earth with stately tread or humbly creep -- witness whether I am ever silent, morning or evening, by hill or valley, fountain or fresh shade, which my song has made vocal and taught his praise.

Hail, universal Lord! Continue to give us only good. And if the night has gathered any evil or concealed it, scatter it now, as light dispels the dark!" So they prayed in their innocence, and firm peace and accustomed calm soon returned to their thoughts.

They hurried to their morning work among the sweet dews and flowers. Where rows of fruit trees had reached too far with their pampered branches, needing hands to trim their fruitless embrace, they pruned them.
Or they led the vine to wed her elm, and she, like a bride, twined her arms around him, bringing her dowry of clustered grapes to adorn his bare leaves.

God in Heaven watched them at work with pity, and called to Raphael, the sociable spirit who had once traveled with Tobias and secured his marriage with the seven-times-widowed bride. "Raphael," God said, "you hear what trouble Satan, having escaped from Hell through the dark abyss, has caused in Paradise, and how he disturbed this human pair last night. He plans to ruin all of humanity through them at once. Go then.
Spend half this day as a friend conversing with Adam. Find him in whatever bower or shade he retreats to from the noonday heat, taking rest or refreshment.
Bring up conversation that may remind him of his happy state -- that his happiness is within his own power and left to his own free will, which though free is mutable.

Warn him to be careful and not grow overconfident. Tell him also about his danger and from whom it comes -- what enemy, lately fallen from Heaven, is now plotting the fall of others from a similar state of bliss.

Not by violence -- for that shall be resisted -- but by deceit and lies. Let Adam know this, so that if he willfully transgresses, he cannot claim surprise, saying he was not advised or forewarned." So spoke the Eternal Father, fulfilling all justice. Without delay, the winged saint received his charge. From among the thousands of celestial Ardors where he stood veiled with gorgeous wings, he sprang up lightly and flew through the midst of Heaven.

The angelic choirs parted on each side to make way through the entire road of Heaven. At last he reached the gate of Heaven, which opened on golden hinges of its own accord, as the divine sovereign Architect had designed it. From there, no cloud or star, however small, blocked his sight.
He could see clearly the Earth, the garden of God, and its cedar-crowned hills. It was like when Galileo's telescope, still uncertain, observes what seem like lands and regions on the moon.

Or like a pilot who, from among the Cyclades islands, first spots Delos or Samos as a cloudy shape on the horizon. Down Raphael flew in swift descent, sailing between worlds through the vast ethereal sky, now riding polar winds, now fanning his way through the gentle air.

When he came within the range of soaring eagles, he appeared to all the birds like a phoenix, that legendary sole bird gazed at by all, flying to the Egyptian city of Thebes to enshrine its remains in the sun's bright temple. On the eastern cliff of Paradise he landed and returned to his proper shape -- a six-winged Seraph. Two wings covered each broad shoulder, draping over his chest with regal ornament. The middle pair girded his waist like a starry belt, with feathered covering around his loins and thighs in downy gold and Heaven-dipped colors.

The third pair of wings shaded his feet from each heel with sky-tinted plumage. Like Mercury he stood and shook his feathers, filling the whole area with heavenly fragrance. Every angel on guard duty recognized him immediately and rose in honor of his rank and his important mission.

They guessed he was bound on some high errand. He passed their glittering tents and now entered the blissful field, walking through groves of myrrh and flowering cassia, nard, and balm -- a wilderness of sweet scents.

Nature here played freely in her prime, pouring forth wild beauty beyond any rule or art, in enormous, unbounded bliss. Adam spotted him coming through the spice forest from where he sat at the door of his cool bower, while the midday sun shot its burning rays straight down to warm the Earth's interior -- more warmth than Adam needed.
Eve was inside, preparing savory fruits for their noon meal -- fruits to please a true appetite, and nectarous drinks from milky streams, berries, or grapes between courses.

Adam called to her. "Come quickly, Eve! Come see something worth seeing! Eastward among those trees, what a glorious shape comes this way, moving like another dawn risen at midday. Perhaps some great messenger from Heaven brings us a message and will honor us today by being our guest. Go with speed and bring out whatever our stores contain. Pour out abundance, fit to honor and welcome our heavenly visitor. We can well afford to give back generously from our great gifts, given so generously. When Nature is unburdened, she only grows more fruitful.

This teaches us not to be stingy." Eve replied: "Adam, you are Earth's sacred prototype, inspired by God! There is no need for great preparation where abundance, ripe for use, hangs on the stalk in all seasons. Only what we store by careful preserving firms and ripens. But I will hurry and from every branch, bush, plant, and juiciest gourd will pluck such delicacies to entertain our angel guest that he shall acknowledge God has distributed his bounties on Earth as generously as in Heaven."
So saying, she turned with eager looks, her mind set on what to choose for the finest dishes, how to arrange them so that one taste would follow another, each one enhanced by pleasing variety.

She busied herself and gathered from every tender stalk whatever all-bearing Mother Earth yields -- fruit of every kind, whether from India East or West, or from the Mediterranean shore, from the lands around the Black Sea, or from the Carthaginian coast, or wherever King Alcinous ruled.
Fruits with rough or smooth skin, bearded husk or shell, she gathered in great abundance and heaped them generously on the table.

For drink she crushed grapes into mild, harmless juice and mixed sweet beverages from berries, pressing sweet kernels into smooth creams. She lacked nothing for proper vessels, and she strewed the ground with roses and fragrant herbs. Meanwhile, our great first father went forth to meet his godlike guest. He was unaccompanied by any retinue except his own complete perfection. His state was all within himself -- more solemn than the tedious pomp that attends princes, with their long train of horses, gold-covered grooms, dazzling the crowd and making everyone gape.

As Adam drew nearer, though not awed, he approached with respectful humility, bowing low as to a superior nature, and spoke: "Native of Heaven -- for no other place could contain such a glorious form -- since by descending from your heavenly thrones you have deigned to briefly leave those happy places and honor ours, please join us -- we are only two, yet by sovereign gift we possess this spacious ground.
Rest in that shady bower and sit and taste what the garden offers at its best, until this midday heat has passed and the sun grows cooler toward evening."
The angelic Virtue answered mildly: "Adam, this is exactly why I came. Nor are you such a lowly creature, nor is this such a lowly place, that it might not often invite heavenly spirits to visit you.

Lead on then to your bower. For these midday hours until evening rises, I am at your disposal." So they came to the forest lodge that smiled like Pomona's arbor, decorated with flowers and sweet scents. But Eve, unadorned except by herself, stood there to welcome her heavenly guest -- more lovely than any woodland nymph, or the fairest goddess imagined of the three who competed naked on Mount Ida.
She needed no veil, being proof against improper thoughts. No unworthy thought altered her expression. The angel bestowed on her the greeting "Hail"
-- the same holy greeting long afterward used for the blessed Mary, the second Eve.
"Hail, Mother of humanity, whose fruitful womb shall fill the world with more children than these various fruits from God's trees have heaped upon this table!"

Their table was a raised turf, with mossy seats around it. On its broad surface, every kind of fruit was piled from side to side -- all the abundance of autumn, though spring and autumn danced hand in hand here.

They talked for a while. No fear of dinner growing cold. Then our host began: "Heavenly stranger, please taste these gifts, which our Provider, from whom all perfect good descends without measure, has caused the earth to produce for us as food and delight.

Perhaps this food seems poor compared to what spiritual beings eat. But I know only this: one Heavenly Father provides for all." The angel replied: "Therefore what he gives -- praised be he forever -- may be found acceptable even to the purest spirits.
Angelic beings require nourishment just as your rational nature does. Both contain within them every lower faculty of sense, by which they hear, see, smell, touch, and taste.

In tasting, they digest and assimilate, turning physical substance into spiritual. For know that whatever was created needs to be sustained and nourished. The grosser elements feed the purer: earth feeds the sea, earth and sea feed air, air feeds the ethereal fires, with the moon being lowest of these. This explains those spots on the moon -- unpurified vapors not yet converted to its substance.

Nor does the moon fail to send nourishment upward to the higher spheres in moist exhalations. The sun, which gives light to all, receives in return nourishment from all in the form of moist vapors, and each evening feeds on the ocean.

Though in Heaven the Trees of Life bear ambrosial fruit and vines yield nectar, though we brush sweet dew from the branches each morning and find the ground covered with pearly grain, still God has varied his bounty here with new delights that may compare with Heaven. And do not think I shall be fussy about tasting them." So they sat down.

The angel ate, and not merely in appearance, nor in some mystical way as some theologians explain, but with genuine hunger and real digestive warmth that converted the food. Whatever was left over evaporated easily through his spiritual body.

This should be no more surprising than if an earthly alchemist, using fire on base coal, can turn -- or claims to turn -- the crudest ore into perfect gold. Meanwhile, Eve served them naked and filled their cups with pleasant drinks. O innocence deserving Paradise!

If ever the sons of God had excuse to be captivated at such a sight, it was then. But in those hearts, love without lust reigned, and jealousy was not known -- that tortured state of the wounded lover. When they had eaten and drunk their fill, not burdened but satisfied, a sudden desire arose in Adam.

He would not let this great opportunity pass to learn about things above his world, and about the nature of his visitor, whose radiant form and divine power so far exceeded anything human. He carefully framed his words to the heavenly minister.

"Inhabitant of Heaven, I recognize your favor in this honor done to me, that you should come under my humble roof and condescend to taste these earthly fruits, food not worthy of angels, yet accepted as if you could not more willingly have dined at Heaven's own high feasts."
The winged Hierarch replied. "O Adam, there is one Almighty from whom all things come, and to whom all things return, unless corrupted from their good original.

He created all things to perfection, all from one first substance, endowed with various forms and degrees -- some lower, some higher, and in living things, varying degrees of life. The more refined, spiritual, and pure a substance is, the nearer to God it is placed, or the more it tends toward him. Each operates in its assigned sphere until body works up to spirit, within the proper proportions for each kind. Just as from a root springs the lighter green stalk, then the airier leaves, and finally the bright flower that breathes fragrant spirits -- so flowers and their fruit, which are Man's nourishment, are gradually refined into vital spirits, then animal spirits, then intellectual ones.

These give both life and sense, imagination and understanding. From understanding, the soul receives reason, and reason is her very being. Reason works either through step-by-step logic or through immediate intuition.

The step-by-step kind is most often yours; the intuitive kind is mostly ours. We differ not in kind but only in degree. So do not wonder if I accept and convert this food to my own substance, as you do to yours.

A time may come when humans may share meals with angels and find the fare neither inconvenient nor too light. And from this bodily nourishment, your bodies may eventually turn entirely to spirit, improved by the passage of time.

Winged, you may ascend to the heavens like us, or you may choose to dwell either here or in heavenly paradises. That is, if you remain obedient and keep his love whole and entire. You are his offspring. Meanwhile, enjoy to the full whatever happiness this happy state can hold, for it cannot contain more than this."

The father of humanity replied: "O favorable spirit, gracious guest! You have taught us well the path that might lead our knowledge up the scale of nature from the center to the outermost reaches. By steps we may ascend to God through contemplating his created works.
But tell me, what did you mean by that warning: 'If you remain obedient'? Can we possibly fail in obedience to him, or desert his love?

He formed us from the dust and placed us here, filled to the very limit of what human desire can seek or imagine." The angel said: "Son of Heaven and Earth, listen carefully! That you are happy, thank God. That you continue to be happy, thank yourself -- that is, thank your obedience. There is where the matter stands.

That was the warning given to you. Take note. God made you perfect but not unchangeable. He made you good, but left it in your power to continue being good. He ordained your will to be free by nature, not overruled by inescapable fate or rigid necessity.
He requires our voluntary service, not forced obedience. Forced obedience finds no acceptance with him, nor could it.

For how can hearts that are not free be tested to see whether they serve willingly or not, when they can do nothing but what destiny compels and have no other choice? I myself, and all the angelic host that stand in God's sight, hold our happy state just as you hold yours -- while our obedience holds.
We have no other security. We serve freely because we freely love, as it is within our will to love or not. In this we stand or fall. And some have fallen.

They fell through disobedience, from Heaven to the deepest Hell. O fall -- from what a high state of bliss into what misery!" Our great ancestor said: "Your words, divine instructor, I have heard with greater delight than when Cherubic songs send aerial music from neighboring hills at night. I already knew I was created free in both will and deed.
Yet I was confident that we would never forget to love our Maker and obey him, whose single command is so reasonable. My constant thoughts assured me of this, and still assure me.
But what you have told me about events in Heaven stirs some doubt in me, yet even more desire to hear the full story, if you are willing to tell it.

It must be a remarkable tale, worthy of attentive silence. And we still have much of the day left. The sun has barely finished half its journey and is just beginning the other half across the great arc of Heaven." So Adam made his request. Raphael, after a brief pause of agreement, began. "You lay a great charge on me, O first of men -- a sad and hard task.

For how shall I describe to human understanding the invisible deeds of warring spirits? How, without sadness, relate the ruin of so many once-glorious and perfect beings? How finally reveal the secrets of another world, which perhaps are not lawful to tell? Yet for your benefit, this is permitted.

And what exceeds human comprehension, I shall describe by comparing spiritual things to physical, as best I can -- though what if Earth is but a shadow of Heaven, and things here more alike than we imagine?
This world did not yet exist, and wild Chaos reigned where these Heavens now turn and where Earth now rests balanced on her center.

One day -- for time, though within eternity, still measures all things by present, past, and future -- on such a day as Heaven's great year produces, the entire host of angels, summoned by imperial command, appeared innumerable before the Almighty's throne, coming from all ends of Heaven under their Hierarchs, arranged in bright orders.

Ten thousand times ten thousand banners advanced, streaming in the air between the front and rear lines, marking the different hierarchies, orders, and ranks. Some bore holy symbols and recorded acts of outstanding devotion and love woven in their glittering fabric.

When they stood in circles beyond imagining, circle within circle, the infinite Father, with the Son seated in bliss beside him, spoke from what seemed a flaming mountain whose peak was made invisible by its own brightness. "Hear, all you angels, children of light -- Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, Virtues, Powers! Hear my decree, which shall stand unrevoked.
This day I have begotten him whom I declare my only Son. On this holy hill I have anointed him. You now see him at my right hand. I appoint him your head.
And I have sworn by myself that to him every knee in Heaven shall bow and every tongue confess him Lord. Under his great authority as viceroy, remain united as one, forever happy.

Whoever disobeys him disobeys me, breaks unity, and on that day shall be cast out from God and blessed sight, falling into utter darkness. His place shall be ordained without redemption, without end." So spoke the Almighty, and all seemed pleased.

All seemed so, but not all truly were. That day, like other solemn days, they spent in song and dance around the sacred hill -- a mystical dance that the starry sphere of planets and fixed stars most closely resembles in its intricate, eccentric, interwoven patterns that seem most regular when they appear most irregular.

The divine harmony of their motions smoothed such charming tones that God's own ear listened with delight. Evening now approached -- for we too have our evenings and mornings, ours for pleasant change, not necessity.

From dancing they turned eagerly to sweet feasting. All standing in their circles, tables appeared suddenly, piled with angel food. Rubied nectar flowed in pearl, diamond, and massive gold cups -- fruit of delicious vines, the growth of Heaven.
Reclining on flowers, crowned with fresh garlands, they ate and drank. In sweet communion they drank immortality and joy, free from any risk of excess, where full measure was the only limit.
They feasted before the all-generous King, who showered abundance with open hand, rejoicing in their joy.

chapters.title: Book VI
paragraphs: All night the tireless angel continued his story. Meanwhile, in the obscured east of Heaven, morning began to dawn. But in the blessed regions above, night's shadow falls neither on Heaven nor on the narrative that Raphael, the affable archangel, had been asked to tell.

Adam was eager for more, charmed by his guest's voice, which made the passing of the night seem like a brief twilight. So Raphael continued. "As soon as night passed and dawn's early light appeared in Heaven, the archangel Michael and his powers went forth with trumpets sounding, as God had commanded.

All the faithful angels -- countless multitudes -- stood armed in shining ranks, wearing Heaven's armor of celestial light. Standards were raised, and the embattled host marched onward, led by Michael's brilliant example.

They met the rebel forces on the open plains of Heaven. There stood Satan's army, equally vast, drawn up in formidable array, moving forward to meet God's loyal host. Between the two great armies, the space quickly narrowed. Abdiel, the faithful angel who alone had stood against the whole rebel assembly and returned unshaken, now stepped forward before the host of God.

With fearless voice he confronted Satan face to face. "O Heaven! That such resemblance of the Highest should still serve to cloak such wickedness as yours," Abdiel cried. "But think not that your false claim to equality with God will go unchallenged.
You stand answered now by deeds, not words alone." Without waiting for reply, he struck with all his might.

The blow was like a thunderbolt against Satan's crest. The great rebel staggered back ten enormous paces. Shock ran through the rebel ranks. But the battle was quickly joined on every side, angel against angel, in terrible conflict. Weapons of celestial temper clashed. The noise was like the crash of whole worlds colliding. Sword met sword, shield pressed against shield. The air blazed with fire from their weapons.

Under their feet the ground of Heaven trembled. Neither side gave way easily, for both were made of celestial substance, powerful beyond any earthly measure. Michael himself, leader of Heaven's host, advanced to seek Satan in single combat. The great archangel raised his sword -- that terrible sword forged in God's armory from pure celestial steel. It could cut through the substance of any spirit. He struck Satan with a mighty downward blow.

The sword bit deep, cutting through Satan's right side. For the first time, Satan knew pain. He writhed and twisted, and from the wound flowed ethereal substance -- not blood as mortals know it, but a luminous stream. His angels rushed to bear him from the field. But spirit cannot die.
Quickly the wound closed, and the severed parts rejoined, for their substance was not mortal. Yet Satan's forces fell back that first day. The loyal angels pressed their advantage across the field.
When evening came, both armies rested. The faithful had won the day's battle, but they knew the war was not yet finished. That night, Satan gathered his forces in council.

His humiliation at the day's defeat only fueled his rage. If force alone could not prevail, perhaps cunning might. "My friends," he said to his assembled captains, "do not let today's reversal discourage you.

We have learned our enemy's strength and can now devise better means. I have conceived a new weapon -- one that will give us advantage tomorrow. Our labor shall not be long. Before dawn we shall be ready. What we build will make our enemies wish they had never challenged us."

He ended, and his words brightened their drooping spirits. All admired his invention, and each wished he had thought of it first. Once discovered, it seemed so obvious. Yet before it was found, most would have thought it impossible. Perhaps in future days, if malice should flourish among your race, some human intent on destruction, inspired by devilish cunning, may devise a similar instrument to plague humanity, using it for war and mutual slaughter.
At once they flew from council to the work. Countless hands were ready. In a moment they turned up the soil of Heaven and found beneath it the raw materials of nature in their crude state.
They discovered sulfurous and nitrous compounds, mixed and processed them with subtle skill, reducing them to a black powder, which they stored away.
Others dug up veins of mineral and stone from which they cast their engines and balls of destruction. They prepared reed fuses, dangerous to ignite with a single touch.

Before daybreak, under cover of the aware night, they secretly finished their preparations and set everything in order, arrayed in silence and hidden from view. When fair morning appeared in Heaven, the victorious angels rose and armed for battle. The morning trumpet sang. They formed their ranks in golden armor, a splendid host. Scouts were sent out on every side to locate the distant enemy -- where they were camped, whether they had fled, and whether they were preparing to fight. They soon found the enemy approaching under spread banners, moving slowly but in firm formation.

Zophiel, swiftest of the Cherubim, came flying back and cried aloud in the air. "Arm, warriors! Arm for battle! The enemy we thought had fled is near at hand. He comes determined to fight today. Do not count on his retreat. I see in his face grim resolution and readiness.

Every angel, gird your adamantine armor well. Fit your helmets snugly, grip your shields firmly, held level or high. For I predict today will bring not a drizzling shower but a rattling storm of arrows tipped with fire." So he warned them. They took the alert and quickly formed into order, clear of all impediment. They stood ready for battle when they saw the enemy approaching -- a massive, heavy formation marching forward, hollow in the center and walled with shadowy squadrons on every side to hide their treachery. Both armies halted briefly to face each other. Then suddenly Satan appeared at the head of his forces and was heard commanding loudly. "Vanguard, open the front lines to the right and left! Let all who hate us see how we seek peace and agreement, and how we stand with open arms ready to receive them -- if they accept our offer.

Do not turn back stubbornly. But I doubt they will listen. Nevertheless, let Heaven witness! Heaven will witness soon! We shall freely do our part. You who are stationed in place, do as you have been ordered, and briefly deliver what we propose, loud enough for all to hear."
He had barely finished this mocking speech, full of double meaning, when the front lines divided right and left, each flank pulling back.
