It was not yet in any horrible den or dismal shade, nor was it harmful yet. On the grassy ground, fearless and unfeared, it slept. Satan entered through its mouth, possessing its brute senses, heart, and head. He inspired it with intelligent purpose, but did not disturb its sleep, waiting hidden for the approach of morning.

Now, when sacred dawn began to rise in Eden over the moist, incense-breathing flowers, and all things that breathe sent up silent praise from Earth's great altar to the Creator, filling his presence with grateful fragrance, the human pair came forth and joined their voices to the choir of creatures that lacked speech. Having done this, they shared the best hour for sweetest scents and air.

Then they discussed how to organize their day's work best, for their garden grew faster than two pairs of hands could manage. Eve spoke first: "Adam, we may labor as we will to tend this garden -- our pleasant appointed task -- but until more hands come to help us, the work outgrows our efforts. What we trim, prune, prop, or bind by day, one or two nights of wild growth undoes, defying our care and going back to wilderness. Let me suggest something.

Let us divide our work. You go where your choice leads or where need is greatest -- whether to train the woodbine around this arbor or direct the ivy where to climb. Meanwhile I will go to that bed of roses mixed with myrtle to find what needs attention until noon.

For while we work so near each other all day, no wonder if looks and smiles interrupt us, or if some casual conversation draws our attention away. Our work comes to little, though we started early, and the supper hour arrives unearned."

Adam gently answered: "Sole Eve, my companion beyond compare, above all living creatures dear! You have proposed well, and your thoughts show proper concern for how we might best fulfill the work God has assigned us. I shall not leave you unpraised for this, for nothing is lovelier in a woman than to care about domestic good and to promote good works in her husband.

Yet God has not imposed labor so strictly that he forbids us refreshment when we need it -- whether food or conversation between tasks, the food of the mind, or this sweet exchange of looks and smiles. Smiles flow from reason, which brutes lack, and they are love's nourishment.

Love is not the lowest purpose of human life. For God made us not for tedious toil but for delight, and delight joined with reason. These paths and bowers, I am confident our combined efforts will easily keep from wilderness, at least as wide as we need to walk, until younger hands before long come to help us. But if my company has grown tiresome and you could use a short absence --

sometimes solitude is the best society, and brief separation makes the return sweeter. But I have another concern: that harm may befall you if we separate. You know what we have been warned about -- the malicious enemy who envies our happiness, and who, despairing of his own, seeks to bring us grief and shame through sly attack. He is somewhere nearby, no doubt, watching with greedy hope for his best chance to catch us apart.
Our separation would make his task hopeless, for together we could quickly aid each other. Whether his plan is to turn us from God or to destroy our married love, which perhaps arouses his envy most,

or something worse -- do not leave the faithful side that gave you life and still protects you. A wife, where danger or dishonor lurks, is safest and most fitting by her husband's side, who guards her or endures the worst alongside her."

Eve, with the virgin dignity of one who loves but feels some injury, replied with sweet, firm composure: "Offspring of Heaven and Earth, Lord of all the Earth! That we have such an enemy who seeks our ruin, I learned from you and from the parting angel, whose words I overheard while I stood behind in a shady corner as the evening flowers were closing.

But that you should therefore doubt my firmness toward God or toward you, because we have an enemy who may tempt it -- this I did not expect to hear. You do not fear his violence, since we are spirits and cannot suffer death or pain from such attacks, nor can we fail to resist them.

Then it is his fraud you fear. This plainly implies that you equally fear my firm faith and love can be shaken or seduced by his deceit. How could such thoughts find a home in your heart, Adam -- such mistrust of her so dear to you?"

Adam replied with soothing words: "Daughter of God and Man, immortal Eve -- for such you are, sinless and blameless -- I am not distrusting you when I discourage your absence from my sight. I only wish to prevent the attempt itself from being made by our enemy.

For he who tempts, even unsuccessfully, dishonors the one tempted by implying they are thought corruptible. You yourself would resent such an insult with scorn and anger, even if the temptation failed. So do not misjudge me if I try to keep such an affront from you alone, which our enemy, though bold, would hardly dare attempt against us both together.

Or if he dared, the first assault would fall on me. Do not underestimate his malice and false cunning. He must be subtle indeed to have seduced angels. And do not think my help unnecessary. I draw strength from the influence of your presence. In your sight I become more wise, more watchful, more strong. Shame of being overcome while you watch would raise my utmost effort and unite all my powers."

"Why should you not feel the same when I am present, and choose your trial with me -- the best witness of your tested virtue?" So spoke Adam in his domestic care and married love. But Eve, who felt he attributed too little to her sincere faith, renewed her reply sweetly.

"If this is our condition -- to live in such a narrow space, hemmed in by a foe who may be subtle or violent, and we are not equipped to defend ourselves alone, wherever we meet him -- then how are we happy, living always in fear of harm?

But harm cannot come before sin. If our enemy merely tempts us, it only insults his own estimate of our integrity. That insult reflects no dishonor on us but turns foul on him. Why then should we avoid or fear it, when by proving his suspicion false we would gain double honor, inward peace, and the favor of Heaven as our witness?

And what is faith, love, or virtue if never tested -- if it can only exist when supported by someone else? Let us not think our Maker left our happy state so imperfect and insecure that it cannot withstand a challenge, whether we face it alone or together.

Fragile indeed would our happiness be if that were so. And Eden would be no Eden if so easily exposed." To this Adam replied fervently: "O Woman, all things are best as God's will ordained them. His creating hand left nothing imperfect or deficient in all his works -- much less in Man, or in anything that might secure his happy state. He is secure from outward force. The danger lies within himself, yet it lies within his own power to control.

No harm can come to him against his will. But God left the will free. For what obeys Reason is free, and Reason he made right. But he warned Reason to be always alert, lest it be surprised by some fair-appearing good and make a wrong judgment, misinforming the will to do what God has expressly forbidden.

It is not mistrust but tender love that urges me to remind you often, and you should remind me too. We stand firm yet are capable of swerving, since Reason might conceivably meet some plausible illusion devised by our enemy, and fall into deception without the strictest vigilance, as we have been warned.

Do not seek temptation. It is better to avoid it, and most likely to succeed if you stay with me. Trial will come without your seeking it. Would you prove your constancy? First prove your obedience. Who can verify the other quality without seeing you actually tested?

But if you think trial unsought may find us both more alert than my warning seems to suggest, then go. Your staying here against your will distances you from me more than going. Go in your native innocence. Rely on what virtue you have. Summon all of it!

For God has done his part toward you. Now do yours." So spoke the father of humanity. But Eve, though submissive, persisted with her final reply: "With your permission then, and forewarned especially by your own concluding words -- that our trial, when least expected, may find us far less prepared -- I go all the more willingly. And I do not much expect a foe so proud will first seek out the weaker target.

If he does, his failure will shame him all the more." So saying, she withdrew her hand softly from her husband's. Like a light woodland nymph -- an Oread or Dryad, or one of Diana's attendants -- she made for the groves. But Diana herself she surpassed in grace and goddess-like bearing, though not armed like Diana with bow and quiver, but with simple gardening tools that primitive art, not yet knowing fire, had formed, or that angels had brought.

She most resembled Pales or Pomona -- Pomona when she fled from Vertumnus, or Ceres in her prime, still a maiden untouched by the sorrow of Proserpine's loss. Adam's eyes followed her with ardent longing, delighted but wishing she would stay.
Again and again he urged her to return quickly. She as often promised to be back by noon at the bower, with everything prepared for their midday meal or afternoon rest.

O much-deceived, much-disappointed, hapless Eve! Your presumed return will prove tragically wrong. From that hour you never again found sweet rest or safe repose in Paradise. Such an ambush, hidden among sweet flowers and shades, waited with hellish venom to intercept your path, or send you back stripped of your innocence, your faith, and your happiness!

For now, since the first break of dawn, the Fiend, in the outward form of a mere serpent, had come forth. He was on his hunt for the only two human beings, but in them the entire future race -- his intended prey.

In bower and field he searched, wherever any garden plot or grove lay more pleasantly arranged, where the pair might be tending their plants or enjoying their favorite places. He searched by fountain and shady stream for both of them, but wished he might find Eve alone. He wished, but without hope of what so rarely happened. Then, to his wish and beyond his hope, he spied Eve alone -- veiled in a cloud of fragrance where she stood, half-hidden as the roses bloomed thickly around her, their blush matching her own glow. She was stooping to support each flower on its slender stalk -- heads that, though bright with carnation, purple, azure, or gold, drooped unsupported. She tied them gently with myrtle bands, all the while unaware that she herself, though the fairest unsupported flower, was now so far from her best support, with the storm so near.

He drew nearer, making his way through many a path of the stateliest covering -- cedar, pine, or palm. Then, now bold, now hidden, now visible, he moved among thick-woven flower beds and arbors, approaching Eve's handiwork.
This spot was more delightful than the fabled gardens of restored Adonis, or famous Alcinous who hosted Odysseus, or that real garden where wise Solomon kept company with his fair Egyptian queen.

He admired the place greatly, but the person even more. Like a city-dweller long confined among crowded houses and foul air who steps out on a summer morning to breathe among pleasant villages and farms, delighting in everything he encounters --

the smell of grain, of fresh-cut grass, of cows or dairy -- every rural sight and sound. And if by chance a lovely maiden with nymph-like grace walks past, what pleased before pleases him all the more. She above all sums up all delight in her appearance.

Such pleasure the Serpent took in viewing this flowery spot, this sweet retreat of Eve, alone so early. Her heavenly form, angelic but softer and more feminine, her graceful innocence, every movement, every least gesture, overpowered his malice. Her presence momentarily stripped his fierceness of its fierce intent, overwhelming it with a sweet, painful beauty.

For a time the Evil One stood abstracted from his own evil. He remained stupidly good for the moment, disarmed of malice, hatred, envy, and revenge. But the fire of Hell that always burns within him, even in the midst of Heaven, quickly ended his delight. The sight of pleasure meant only for others, not for him, tormented him more than ever. Soon he recollected his fierce hatred and stirred up all his thoughts of destruction, congratulating himself as he spoke.

"Thoughts, where have you led me? With what sweet compulsion was I carried away, forgetting what brought me here? Hate, not love, brought me -- not hope of enjoying Paradise, but only the desire to destroy all pleasure except the pleasure of destroying. All other joy is lost to me. Then let me not miss this opportunity, which now smiles on me. The woman stands alone, open to every attempt. Her husband -- I can see far around -- is nowhere near. His greater intelligence and his heroic strength, though earthly, I prefer to avoid.

He is a formidable foe, not easily dismissed, since Hell has weakened me with such pain. She is fair, divinely fair, fit to be loved by gods. Not terrible, though there is terror in love and beauty -- but not enough to resist the stronger hate I bring, hate masked by a show of love.

That show is the path I now take toward her ruin." So spoke the enemy of humankind, enclosed in the Serpent's body -- a wicked occupant! He moved toward Eve. He did not crawl on his belly along the ground as serpents have done since, but rose up on his coiled base, fold above fold, a surging maze of rising loops. His head was crested high, his eyes like carbuncles.

His burnished neck of green and gold stood erect amid his spiraling coils, which floated over the grass in elegant excess. His shape was pleasing and lovely -- never was there a lovelier serpent, not even those into which Hermione and Cadmus were transformed in Illyria, or the god at Epidaurus, or the forms taken by Ammon or Capitoline Jupiter.

One appeared with Olympias, the other with the woman who bore Scipio, the height of Rome. With a sidelong, indirect approach, like one seeking access but fearful of interrupting, the Serpent worked his way toward Eve. Like a ship skillfully steered near a river's mouth or headland, where the wind frequently shifts and the steersman constantly adjusts the sails --

so he varied his winding course, curling many a playful loop in Eve's sight to catch her eye. She, busy at her work, heard the rustling of leaves but paid it no mind, being used to such behavior from the animals. They were more obedient to her call than the beasts Circe enchanted.

Now bolder, uncalled, he stood before her, but as if in admiring wonder. He bowed his turreted crest repeatedly and stroked his smooth, enameled neck, fawning. He licked the ground where she stepped. His gentle, wordless display at last caught Eve's eye. Glad of her attention, with his serpent tongue -- whether organic or moved by impulse of vocal air -- he began his fraudulent temptation.

"Do not be amazed, sovereign Mistress -- if amazement is even possible for you, who are amazement itself! Still less should you arm those looks, that heaven of mildness, with displeasure at my approach and insatiable gaze. I come alone, nor have I feared your awesome brow, all the more awesome in this secluded setting.

Fairest image of your fair Maker! All living things gaze upon you. All things are yours by gift. They worship your celestial beauty with rapture! Best seen where universally admired. But here in this wild enclosure, among these beasts -- crude observers too shallow to appreciate half of what is fair in you -- who sees you? Only one man. And what is one? You should be seen as a goddess among gods, worshiped and served by angels numberless, your daily attendants."

So the Tempter flattered, tuning his opening speech. His words made their way into Eve's heart, though she marveled greatly at the voice. At length, not without surprise, she answered: "What can this mean? Language that men speak, produced by the tongue of a beast, and expressing human understanding?

The first of these abilities I thought was denied to beasts. God, on their creation day, created them mute to all articulate speech. The second I am uncertain about, for in their looks and actions, considerable reason often appears.

You, Serpent, I knew as the most cunning beast of all the field, but not endowed with human voice. Double then this miracle, and tell me: how did you go from mute to speaking? And how did you become so friendly toward me, above all other animal kinds that I see daily?

Tell me, for such a wonder deserves attention." The crafty Tempter replied: "Empress of this fair world, radiant Eve! It is easy for me to tell you everything you command. And you deserve to be obeyed.

I was at first like other beasts that graze the trampled grass. My thoughts were base and low, concerned with nothing but food and mating. I perceived nothing higher. Then one day, roaming the field, I happened to see a fine tree at a distance, loaded with fruit of the most beautiful mixed colors, red and gold. I drew nearer to look.
A savory smell blown from its branches pleased my appetite more than the scent of the sweetest fennel or the milk-dripping teats of a ewe or goat at evening, not yet suckled by their young at play.
To satisfy the sharp desire I felt to taste those fair apples, I resolved not to delay. Hunger and thirst, powerful persuaders, were quickened by the scent of that enticing fruit and urged me keenly.

I wound myself around the mossy trunk, for the branches were too high from the ground -- they would require your full reach or Adam's. All the other beasts that saw the fruit stood around with the same longing desire and envy, but could not reach it.

Once up in the tree, surrounded by plenty hanging temptingly close, I did not hold back. I plucked and ate my fill with such pleasure as I had never found at any feeding or fountain before. When at last I was satisfied, I soon perceived a strange change in myself -- a new power of reason in my inner faculties, and the gift of speech, which before long followed, though I kept this outward serpent form.

From then on I turned my thoughts to high and deep matters. I considered all things visible in Heaven, on Earth, or in between -- all things fair and good. But all that is fair and good, united in your divine likeness and in your heavenly beauty, I beheld. No fairness anywhere equals or compares to yours! This compelled me, perhaps rudely, to come here and gaze at you, worshiping you as rightfully declared the sovereign of all creatures, the universal queen!"

So spoke the cunning, spirit-possessed Snake. Eve, even more amazed, replied without caution: "Serpent, your excessive praise raises doubt about the real virtue of that fruit you claim you first tested. But tell me, where does this tree grow? How far from here?

For many are God's trees that grow in Paradise, various in kind, yet unknown to us. Our choice is so abundant that a great store of fruit hangs untouched, still perfect, until the human population grows to match the provision and more hands help to ease Nature of her burden."

The crafty Serpent, cheerful and eager, replied: "Empress, the way is short and easy. Beyond a row of myrtles, on a flat spot by a fountain, past one small thicket of fragrant myrrh and balm -- if you will accept my guidance, I can bring you there quickly." "Lead on," said Eve. He led, swiftly rolling himself forward in tangles, making what was crooked seem straight -- swift to mischief. Hope lifted his spirits and joy brightened his crest. He was like a will-o'-the-wisp, that wandering flame formed from compressed, oily vapor that the cold night condenses and kindles through agitation. It often blazes with misleading light, they say attended by some evil spirit, leading the bewildered night-wanderer from his way into bogs, marshes, ponds, or pools,

where, swallowed up and lost, he is far from rescue. Just so the sinister Snake glittered as he led Eve, our trusting mother, in fraud to the Tree of Prohibition, the root of all our misery. When she recognized it, she said to her guide:

"Serpent, we might have saved ourselves the trip. This is fruitless for me, though the tree has fruit in abundance. The credit for its supposed virtue rests with you -- wonderful indeed, if it truly caused such effects. But of this tree we may not taste or touch.

God has commanded it, and left that command as the sole word of his voice requiring obedience. Everything else we are free to determine for ourselves. Our reason is our law." The Tempter replied with cunning: "Indeed! Has God then said that you shall not eat the fruit of all these garden trees, yet declared you lords of everything in Earth and air?"

Eve, still sinless, answered: "Of the fruit of every tree in the garden we may eat. But of the fruit of this fair tree in the middle of the garden, God has said: 'You shall not eat of it, nor shall you touch it, lest you die.'"

She had barely spoken, briefly, when the Tempter, now more boldly, put on a new act. With a show of passion and zealous love for humanity, and indignation at the wrong done to them, he seemed moved to passionate speech, as if about to begin some great oration.

Like a famous speaker in ancient Athens or free Rome, where eloquence once flourished and is now silent, who rises to address some great cause and first stands collected in himself, while every gesture and movement wins the audience's attention even before he speaks --

sometimes beginning at the height of emotion, brooking no delay for preamble in his zeal for justice -- so the Tempter, standing, moving, growing in stature, and fully impassioned, began: "O sacred, wise, wisdom-giving Plant, Mother of knowledge! Now I feel your power clearly within me -- the power not only to understand things in their causes but to trace the ways of the highest agents, however wise they are deemed.

Queen of this universe! Do not believe those rigid threats of death. You shall not die! How could you? From the fruit? It gives you life and knowledge. From the one who threatens? Look at me -- I have touched and tasted it, yet I live, and have achieved a more perfect life than Fate intended for me, by venturing beyond my station.

Shall what is open to beasts be closed to Man? Or will God be angry over such a trivial offense? Would he not rather praise your fearless courage, when the threat of death -- whatever death may be -- did not deter you from pursuing what might lead to a happier life, to knowledge of good and evil?

If evil is real, should it not be known, since it can then be more easily avoided? God therefore cannot harm you and be just. If he is not just, he is not God, and should not be feared or obeyed. Your very fear of death removes the thing you fear.

Why was this forbidden? Only to keep you in awe. Only to keep you humble and ignorant, as his worshipers. He knows that on the day you eat of it, your eyes, which seem so clear yet are still dim, will be perfectly opened and cleared. You shall be like gods, knowing both good and evil as they do.

That you should become like gods, since I as a beast have become like a man in understanding, is only fair proportion. I from brute to human; you from human to gods. So perhaps you will die -- by putting off the human to put on the divine. Death that is wished for, though it is called a threat, can bring nothing worse than this.

And what are gods that Man may not become the same, sharing in this god-like food? The gods came first and use that advantage to make us believe everything comes from them. I question this. I see this fair Earth, warmed by the Sun, producing every kind of thing.

But the gods produce nothing. If they created everything, then why did they enclose the knowledge of good and evil in this tree, so that whoever eats it immediately gains wisdom without their permission? Where is the offense in Man's gaining knowledge?

What can your knowledge hurt him, or this tree impart against his will, if everything is his? Or is it envy? And can envy dwell in heavenly hearts? These reasons and many more show why you need this fair fruit.

Goddess in human form, reach out and freely taste!" He finished. His words, stuffed with deceit, found all too easy an entrance into her heart. She gazed at the fruit, which by itself was tempting enough to look at. The sound of his persuasive words, filled with what seemed like reason and truth, still rang in her ears.

Meanwhile noon arrived and awakened an eager appetite, stirred by the savory smell of that fruit. Her growing desire to touch or taste it drew her longing eyes. Yet first she paused a while and mused to herself.

"Great must be your virtues, best of fruits, though kept from Man and worthy of admiration. Your taste, too long avoided, gave eloquence to the mute serpent at the first try, and taught a tongue not made for speech to speak your praise.

Your praise even he who forbids your use does not conceal, for he names you the Tree of Knowledge -- knowledge of both good and evil. He forbids us to taste! But his prohibition actually commends you more, since it implies the good you confer and shows our need.

For good that is unknown is surely not possessed. And good possessed but unknown is as good as not possessed at all. Plainly then, what does he forbid but knowledge? He forbids us to be wise! Such prohibitions have no binding force. But if death binds us with further penalties, what good is our inward freedom? 'On the day we eat of this fair fruit, our doom is that we shall die!'

How does the Serpent die then? He has eaten and lives, and knows, and speaks, and reasons, and shows intelligence that was not there before. Was death invented only for us? Or is this intellectual food denied to us and reserved only for beasts?

For beasts it seems, yet the one beast that first tasted does not begrudge it but joyfully brings the benefit to me -- an unsuspected, trustworthy guide, friendly to humanity and far from any deceit or treachery. What should I fear then? What do I really know to fear under this ignorance of good and evil, of God or death, of law or penalty?

Here grows the cure for all of this. This divine fruit, fair to the eye, inviting to taste, powerful to make one wise -- what stops me then from reaching out and feeding both body and mind at once?" So saying, her reckless hand in an evil hour reached for the fruit. She plucked it and she ate.

The Earth felt the wound. Nature, from her seat, sighed through all her works and gave signs of grief that all was lost. The guilty Serpent slunk back into the thicket -- and well he might. For Eve, now wholly focused on the taste, noticed nothing else. Such delight, or so it seemed, she had never known in any fruit before -- whether real or merely imagined through the high expectation of knowledge. Thoughts of becoming a goddess were not far from her mind.

Greedily she ate without restraint, not knowing she was eating death. Satisfied at last and exhilarated as if intoxicated with wine, she cheerfully began to say to herself: "O sovereign, precious tree of all trees in Paradise! Blessed in your powers to give wisdom, until now kept obscure and in low reputation.

Your fair fruit has hung as if created for no purpose. But from now on, every morning without fail, I will tend you with care and song and due praise, easing the heavy burden of your full branches, freely offered to all.

Until, nourished by you, I grow mature in knowledge like the gods, who know all things -- though others envy what they cannot give. For if the gift were theirs, it would not have grown here. I owe experience next to you, best guide. Without following you, I would have remained in ignorance. You open wisdom's way and give access, though wisdom itself stays hidden.

And perhaps I am hidden too. Heaven is high, high and remote, too far to see clearly each thing on Earth. And perhaps other concerns have diverted our great Forbidder from keeping constant watch, safe as he may feel with all his spies around him. But how shall I appear to Adam? Shall I reveal my change to him and share this full happiness, or keep the advantage of this knowledge to myself as a secret power? By adding what I lack in my female nature, I might draw his love more strongly and perhaps even make myself -- a thing not undesirable -- sometimes his superior, since as an inferior, who is truly free? This plan may work. But what if God has seen everything, and death follows? Then I would be no more!

And Adam, wedded to another Eve, would live and enjoy life while I am extinct -- a thought that is itself a death! Then I am resolved. Adam shall share with me in happiness or misery. I love him so dearly that I could endure all deaths with him, but without him I could not live."

So saying, she turned from the tree. But first she bowed in reverence to it, as to the power that dwelt within, whose presence had infused this tree with knowledge-giving sap derived from nectar, the drink of gods. Meanwhile Adam, who had been waiting anxiously for her return, had woven a garland of the choicest flowers to crown her hair and her rural labors,

as reapers often crown their harvest queen. He had promised himself great joy and new comfort from her return, so long delayed. Yet often his heart, sensing something wrong, misgave him. He felt the faltering rhythm of unease.

He went forth to meet her along the path she had taken that morning when they first parted. Near the Tree of Knowledge he had to pass. There he met her, just returning from the tree. In her hand she held a branch of the fairest fruit, freshly picked, smiling with a dewy blush and diffusing an ambrosial scent.

She hurried toward him. In her face, guilt came as prologue, and she wore an apology too ready on her lips. She addressed him with smooth words: "Have you not wondered, Adam, at my delay? I have missed you, and being deprived of your presence felt an agony of love I had never felt before and shall never feel again. For I never again intend to try what I rashly attempted -- the pain of being absent from your sight. But the cause of my delay has been strange and wonderful to hear.

This tree is not, as we were told, a dangerous tree that opens the way to evil when tasted. Instead it has a divine power to open the eyes and make gods of those who taste it. And it has been tasted by such a being: the wise Serpent, either not bound by the same restriction or not obeying it, has eaten of the fruit. He has become, not dead as we were threatened, but from that point endowed with human voice and human reasoning, arguing persuasively enough that I too have tasted. And I have found the effects match his claims: my eyes, once dim, are now opened wider. My spirits are expanded, my heart enlarged, and I feel myself growing toward godhood. I sought this chiefly for you, since without you I could despise it.

For happiness shared with you is happiness to me. Without your share, it would be tedious and soon hateful. So taste it too, so that equal destiny may join us in equal joy and equal love. Otherwise, if you do not taste, the different degree between us may separate us. Then it would be too late for me to give up my divine status for your sake, when Fate will not allow it."

So Eve told her story with a cheerful face, though a feverish flush glowed in her cheeks. Adam, the moment he heard of Eve's fatal trespass, stood thunderstruck, blank and pale with horror. A chill ran through his veins and all his joints went slack.

From his nerveless hand the garland he had woven for Eve dropped, and all the faded roses scattered. Speechless and pale he stood, until at last he broke the inner silence with these words: "O fairest of Creation, last and best of all God's works! Creature in whom everything holy, divine, good, lovely, or sweet that sight or thought could imagine came together in perfection!

How are you lost! How suddenly lost, ruined, corrupted, and now given over to death! Rather, how could you yield to transgression and violate the strict prohibition, the sacred forbidden fruit! Some accursed trick of an unknown enemy has deceived you, and ruined me along with you. For my resolution is fixed: with you I am determined to die.

How can I live without you? How could I give up your sweet companionship, your love so dearly shared, and live again forlorn in these wild woods? Even if God created another Eve and I could spare another rib, the loss of you would never leave my heart. No! I feel the bond of Nature drawing me -- flesh of my flesh, bone of my bone you are. From your fate mine shall never be separated, in happiness or in misery."

Having said this, as one who recovers from a sad shock and submits to what seems beyond remedy, he turned to Eve in calm words: "You have done a bold thing, daring Eve, and provoked great danger by venturing so far. It would have been bad enough merely to covet and gaze at that sacred, forbidden fruit. How much worse to taste it!

But what is done cannot be recalled or undone -- not even by God Almighty, nor by Fate. Yet perhaps you shall not die. Perhaps the act is not so terrible now that the fruit has already been profaned -- first touched by the Serpent, made common and no longer sacred before we tasted it.

And the Serpent is not dead from it. He lives, as you said, and has gained a higher degree of life, gaining human understanding. This is a strong incentive for us to expect a proportional advancement, which can only mean becoming gods, or half-gods.

Nor can I believe that God, wise Creator, though he threatens, would truly destroy us -- his prime creatures, so highly honored, set over all his works. In our fall, everything he created for us would have to fail too, since everything depends on us. So God would have to unmake his creation, undo what he has done, and lose all his labor.

It is not consistent with our idea of God, who though his power could repeat all creation, would be reluctant to abolish us, lest the Adversary triumph and say: 'How fickle God's favorites are! Who can please him long? First he ruined me, now he has ruined humanity. Who will he ruin next?' This would give our enemy material for scorn.

However that may be, I have fixed my lot with yours. I am certain to share the same fate. If death is to be your companion, death is life to me. So powerfully I feel the bond of Nature drawing me to my own --

my own in you, for what you are is mine. Our state cannot be divided. We are one, one flesh. To lose you would be to lose myself." So Adam spoke. And Eve replied: "O glorious proof of surpassing love, noble evidence and supreme example!

Your perfection moves me to try to match it, though I fall short. Adam, from whose dear side I proudly claim to have sprung, I am glad to hear you speak of our union -- one heart, one soul in both. Today's events give good proof of this, declaring you resolved that neither death nor anything worse than death shall separate us, linked in such dear love. You are willing to share one guilt, one consequence with me, if any there be, in tasting this fair fruit,

whose virtue -- for good still proceeds from good, whether directly or by occasion -- has presented this happy test of your love, which would otherwise never have been so wonderfully revealed. If I believed death would actually follow from my attempt, I would choose to bear the worst alone and not persuade you. I would rather die abandoned than make you share a harmful act. This is especially true since I am so recently and remarkably assured of your faithful, unequaled love. But I feel the result to be quite different from death. I feel not death but life increased, opened eyes, new hopes, new joys. The taste seems so divine that everything sweet I have experienced before now seems flat and harsh by comparison.

Based on my experience, Adam, taste freely and banish the fear of death to the winds." So saying, she embraced him and tenderly wept for joy, deeply moved that he had so nobly shown his love by choosing to share divine displeasure or death for her sake.

In return -- for such compliance earned such a reward -- she gave him of that fair, enticing fruit from the branch, with a generous hand. He did not hesitate to eat, against his better knowledge. He was not deceived but overcome by her female charm.

The Earth trembled from its core, as if in birth pangs again. Nature gave a second groan. The sky darkened. Muttering thunder shed some sorrowful drops, weeping at the completion of the original mortal sin. But Adam took no notice, eating his fill. Nor did Eve fear to repeat her earlier trespass, eager to soothe him with her loving company. Now, as if intoxicated with new wine, they both swam in giddy delight. They imagined they felt divinity growing within them, breeding wings to lift them above the Earth in scorn. But that false fruit first displayed a very different effect: it inflamed carnal desire. He began to cast lustful eyes on Eve. She returned his look just as wantonly. They burned with appetite.

Then Adam spoke to Eve in a coaxing tone: "Eve, I see now you have excellent taste, refined and knowledgeable -- no small part of wisdom, since we use the word 'savor' for both meaning and taste, and call the judicious palate wise. I give you credit for today's fine provision.

Much pleasure we lost by abstaining from this delightful fruit until now, never knowing true relish. If such pleasure can be found in forbidden things, I wish that instead of one forbidden tree, there had been ten.

But come, so well refreshed, now let us enjoy ourselves, as is fitting after such delicious fare. For never since the day I first saw you and married you, adorned with all perfections, has your beauty so inflamed my senses as now -- lovelier than ever. This is the bounty of that excellent tree!"

So he said, making no secret of his amorous intent. Eve well understood. Her eyes darted a contagious fire. He seized her hand and led her to a shady bank, thickly roofed overhead with green canopy. There among the flowers -- pansies, violets, asphodel, and hyacinth -- Earth's softest, freshest lap, they lay down together.

They took their fill of love's pleasures, the seal of their shared guilt, the consolation of their sin. Dewy sleep pressed down on them, wearied by their lovemaking. Soon the force of that deceptive fruit -- whose bland, intoxicating vapor had played upon their spirits and confused their inner powers -- was now spent. A heavier, unwholesome sleep, bred from unnatural fumes and troubled by guilty dreams, had weighed upon them. Now it lifted. They rose as if from unrest. Looking at each other, they found their eyes suddenly opened and their minds darkened. Innocence, which had been like a veil shielding them from the knowledge of evil, was gone.

Confidence, natural righteousness, and honor had departed, leaving them naked to guilty shame. He tried to cover himself, but his attempts at covering only exposed more. So Samson, the mighty champion, rose from the treacherous lap of the Philistine Delilah and woke shorn of his strength. They were left destitute, stripped bare of all their virtue. Silent and ashamed, they sat for a long time, as if struck dumb.

At last Adam, though no less ashamed than Eve, forced himself to speak: "O Eve, in an evil hour you listened to that false serpent, whoever taught it to mimic a man's voice. True in bringing about our fall, false in its promised elevation. Since now our eyes are opened indeed, we find that we know both good and evil. Good is lost, and evil has been gained.

Bad fruit of knowledge, if this is what it means to know -- knowing that leaves us naked, stripped of honor, innocence, faith, and purity, our former ornaments now soiled and stained. The signs of base desire are evident in our faces, from which will come an evil harvest.

Even shame, the last of evils, has arrived. The first evils must be close behind. How shall I ever again face God or angel, whose sight once filled me with joy and rapture? Their heavenly forms will now dazzle these earthly eyes with unbearable brightness. Oh, if only I could live here in solitude as a savage, in some dark, obscure glade where the thickest woods block every ray of sun or starlight, spreading broad and deep shade as dark as evening. Cover me, you pines!

Hide me, you cedars, with your countless branches, where I may never see them again! But for now, let us figure out how to hide the parts of each other that seem most shameful and embarrassing to be seen.

Some tree with broad, smooth leaves, sewn together and tied around our waists, may cover our middle parts, so that this newcomer Shame does not settle there and reproach us as unclean." So he advised. Together they went into the thickest woods. They soon chose the fig tree -- not the kind renowned for its fruit, but the kind known to Indians in Malabar or the Deccan, which spreads its arms so broadly that its bent twigs take root in the ground. Daughter trees grow around the mother, forming a pillared shade of high arches with echoing walkways between them.

There the Indian herdsman, avoiding the heat, shelters in the cool and tends his grazing herds through openings cut in the thickest shade. These were the leaves they gathered, broad as Amazonian shields. With what skill they had, they sewed them together to make a belt for their waists -- a vain covering, if it was meant to hide their guilt and shameful dread! How unlike that first naked glory! Just so Columbus found the Americans, similarly dressed in feathered garments -- otherwise naked and wild among the trees on islands and woody shores.

So outfitted, and as they thought partly covering their shame, they sat down to weep. Not just tears rained from their eyes, but fierce inner storms began to rise -- anger, hatred, mistrust, suspicion, and discord. These shook their inward state of mind, once a calm region full of peace, now tossed and turbulent.

For Understanding no longer ruled. The Will no longer heeded Reason's guidance. Both were now in subjection to sensual Appetite, which usurped authority over sovereign Reason from below. From this disordered state, Adam, estranged in look and changed in tone, renewed his speech to Eve.

"If only you had listened to my words and stayed with me as I asked, when that strange desire to wander, this unhappy morning -- I do not know what possessed you -- took hold. We would still be happy, not despoiled of all our good as we are now: shamed, naked, miserable!

Let no one hereafter needlessly seek to prove the faith they owe. When they eagerly seek such proof, take it as a sign they are beginning to fail." Eve, quickly stung by this blame, replied: "What words have you spoken, Adam, harsh as they are!

Do you blame my error, or my desire to wander, as you call it? For all you know, the same thing might have happened with you present, or to you yourself. Had you been there, or here when the attempt was made, you could not have seen through the Serpent's fraud any more than I could, speaking as it did.

There was no known ground of hostility between us and the Serpent, no reason to suspect it meant me harm. Was I never to leave your side? I might as well have stayed there as a lifeless rib. Being what I am, why did you not absolutely command me not to go,

since you knew it was dangerous, as you said? You gave in too easily then. You did not strongly object. In fact, you permitted it, approved it, and cheerfully sent me off. If you had been firm in your objection, neither would I have sinned, nor you with me." Adam, now angry for the first time, replied:

"Is this the love, is this the gratitude you show me, ungrateful Eve? -- love expressed as unchangeable when you were lost and I was not? I could have lived and enjoyed immortal happiness, yet willingly chose death with you!

And now I am blamed as the cause of your sin? Not strict enough in holding you back, it seems. I warned you, I cautioned you, I foretold the danger and the lurking enemy who lay in wait. Beyond that would have been using force,

and force has no place against free will. But your confidence drove you on -- certain you would meet no danger, or that you would find some glorious test of virtue. And perhaps I also erred in admiring too much what seemed so perfect in you, thinking no evil could dare to touch you. Now I regret that error, which has become my crime, and you my accuser. This is what will always happen to the man who, overtrusting a woman's worth, lets her will rule. If she resists restraint,

and then, left to herself, if evil follows, she will blame his weak indulgence first." So they spent the fruitless hours in mutual accusation, neither one condemning themselves. There seemed no end to their pointless quarrel.

chapters.title: Book X
paragraphs: Meanwhile, the terrible and spiteful act of Satan in Paradise -- how he, in the Serpent, had corrupted Eve, and she her husband, to taste the fatal fruit -- was known in Heaven. For what can escape the eye of God, who sees everything, or deceive his omniscient heart? Being wise and just in all things, he had not prevented Satan from testing the mind of Man, who was armed with full strength and free will, completely equipped to detect and repel whatever tricks any enemy or supposed friend might use.

For they still knew, and should have always remembered, the supreme command not to taste that fruit, whoever might tempt them. By disobeying -- and what lesser outcome could there be? -- they incurred the penalty. Through their multiple sins, they deserved to fall.

Up into Heaven from Paradise the angelic guards ascended, silent and sad for Man's sake. They already knew his fallen state. They wondered greatly how the cunning Fiend had entered unseen. As soon as the unwelcome news from Earth arrived at Heaven's gate, all who heard it were displeased. A dim sadness touched even celestial faces, yet mixed with pity, it did not destroy their bliss.

Around the newly arrived guards, the heavenly people gathered in crowds to hear what had happened. They hurried toward the supreme throne to report, with righteous justification for their utmost vigilance -- which was easily approved. Then the Most High Eternal Father, from behind his secret cloud, uttered his voice amid thunder.

"Assembled angels, you Powers returned from your unsuccessful charge -- do not be dismayed or troubled by these tidings from Earth, which your most diligent care could not have prevented. I foretold all this only recently, when the Tempter first crossed the gulf from Hell.

I told you then that he would succeed in his wicked mission. Man would be seduced, flattered out of everything by believing lies against his Maker. No decree of mine contributed to necessitating his fall or touched his free will with even the slightest impulse. I left his will on its own inclination, in even balance. But he has fallen. And now what remains but that the mortal sentence be pronounced upon his transgression -- death, declared on that very day?

He presumes that sentence is already void and empty because it has not yet been carried out, as he feared, by some immediate stroke. But he shall soon discover that forbearance is not acquittal, before the day ends. Justice shall not be returned as if its bounty were scorned.

But whom shall I send to judge them? Whom but you, my Son and Vicegerent? To you I have transferred all judgment, whether in Heaven, Earth, or Hell. It should be clear that I intend mercy combined with justice, sending you who are Man's friend, his designed Mediator, voluntary Ransom, and Redeemer -- Man himself, destined to judge fallen Man."

So spoke the Father. Unfolding his bright glory toward the right hand, his full, unclouded Deity blazed forth on the Son. The Son, resplendent, fully expressed all his Father and answered with divine gentleness.

"Father Eternal, it is yours to decree and mine to carry out your will, supreme both in Heaven and on Earth. In me, your beloved Son, may you always find rest and satisfaction. I go to judge these transgressors on Earth. But you know that whoever is judged, the worst must ultimately fall on me, when the time comes. For I undertook this before you and do not regret it. I claim the right to lessen their doom by taking it upon myself. Yet I shall balance justice with mercy, so as to satisfy both fully and appease you.

I shall need no attendants or retinue. No one needs to witness the judgment except the judged -- those two. The third, best absent, is already condemned by his flight and his rebellion against all law. The physical serpent deserves no formal trial."
So saying, from his radiant seat of supreme glory he rose. Thrones, Powers, Principalities, and Dominions accompanied him to Heaven's gate, from which Eden and all the surrounding coast lay in view.

He descended directly. The speed of gods is beyond time's measure, though the swiftest minutes fly. Now the sun was declining in the west from noon. Gentle breezes, arriving at their appointed hour to cool the Earth, ushered in the evening. He came, cooler now than his wrath, the mild Judge and Intercessor both, to pass sentence on Man. They heard the voice of God walking in the garden, brought to their ears by soft winds while day declined. They heard it and hid themselves among the thickest trees, both man and wife. God, approaching, called aloud to Adam.

"Where are you, Adam? You who used to come joyfully to meet me when you saw me approaching from far off? I miss you here and am not pleased to be greeted with solitude where eager duty once appeared unsought. Have I become less visible, or what change keeps you away, or what circumstance detains you? Come forth!"

He came, and with him Eve, even more reluctant, though she had sinned first. Both were dejected and disheveled. Love was absent from their looks, whether toward God or toward each other. Instead, their faces showed obvious guilt, shame, confusion, despair, anger, stubbornness, hate, and deceit.

Adam, faltering for a long time, finally answered briefly: "I heard you in the garden. Afraid of your voice because I was naked, I hid myself." The gracious Judge replied without scolding: "You have often heard my voice before and were never afraid but always rejoiced. How is it now so dreadful to you? Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree I charged you not to eat from?"
Adam, deeply troubled, replied: "O Heaven! I stand today in a terrible position before my Judge. Either I must take the entire blame upon myself, or accuse the partner of my life.

Her failure, while her faithfulness to me remains, I should conceal and not expose to blame by my complaint. But strict necessity forces me under this terrible constraint, lest both the sin and punishment, however unbearable, fall entirely on my head. And even if I kept silent, you would easily discover what I try to hide. This woman, whom you made to be my help and gave me as your perfect gift -- so good, so fit, so pleasing, so divine that from her hand I could suspect nothing harmful, and whatever she did seemed to justify the deed --

she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate." The Sovereign Presence replied: "Was she your God, that you obeyed her before his voice? Was she made your guide, your superior, or even your equal, that to her you resigned your manhood and the position God set you in above her? She was created from you and for you. Her perfection far exceeded yours in all real dignity. True, she was adorned and lovely, designed to attract your love, but not your submission. Her gifts were the kind that are properly expressed under governance.

It was unfitting for her to rule. That was your role and responsibility, had you known yourself properly." Having said this, he turned briefly to Eve: "Tell me, woman, what have you done?" Sad Eve, nearly overwhelmed with shame, confessing quickly yet without being bold or wordy before her Judge, replied humbly:

"The Serpent deceived me, and I ate." When the Lord God heard this, he proceeded without delay to pass judgment on the accused Serpent, though it was only a brute animal. It could not transfer the guilt to the one who had used it as an instrument of evil and corrupted it from its created purpose. Justly it was cursed as having been corrupted in its very nature. Man did not need to know more than this, and it did not change the nature of Man's own offense. Yet God applied the sentence primarily to Satan, who was first in sin, though in mysterious terms, judged as seemed best at the time.

And upon the Serpent he pronounced this curse: "Because you have done this, you are cursed above all cattle and every beast of the field. Upon your belly you shall crawl, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life.

I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers. Her offspring shall crush your head, and you shall bruise his heel." So spoke this prophecy, later fulfilled when Jesus, Son of Mary the second Eve, saw Satan fall like lightning from Heaven -- Prince of the air. Then, rising from his grave, he stripped the Principalities and Powers of their authority, triumphing over them openly. With his bright ascension, he led captivity captive through the air, Satan's own realm long wrongfully held.

He shall ultimately trample Satan under our feet -- the very one who now foretold this fatal bruising. And to the woman he turned his sentence: "I will greatly multiply your sorrow in conception. In sorrow you shall bring forth children. Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you."

On Adam last he pronounced this judgment: "Because you have listened to your wife's voice and eaten from the tree concerning which I charged you, saying you shall not eat of it -- cursed is the ground for your sake. In sorrow you shall eat from it all the days of your life.

Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you unbidden. You shall eat the herbs of the field. By the sweat of your brow you shall eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of the ground you were taken. Know your origin: you are dust, and to dust you shall return."

So he judged Man -- sent both as Judge and as Savior. The instant stroke of death, declared for that day, he removed to a distant future. Then, pitying how they stood before him naked in air that now must undergo harsh changes, he did not disdain to take on the form of a servant.

As later he would wash his disciples' feet, so now, as father of his family, he clothed their nakedness with skins of beasts -- either killed for this purpose, or like the snake's cast-off skin renewed with a fresh coat. He did not think it beneath him to clothe even his enemies.

Nor did he cover only their outward nakedness with animal skins. Their far more shameful inner nakedness he also clothed with his robe of righteousness, covering them from the Father's sight. Then with swift ascent he returned to his blissful place, received once more into glory, as before. To the Father, though he already knew everything, the Son recounted what had transpired with Man, mixing sweet intercession into the account.

Meanwhile, before all this sinning and judgment had taken place on Earth, within the gates of Hell sat Sin and Death, facing each other inside the gates. The gates now stood wide open, belching outrageous flame far into Chaos, since Sin had opened them for the Fiend to pass through. Sin now spoke to Death.

"O Son, why do we sit here gazing at each other idly while Satan, our great creator, prospers in other worlds and provides a happier home for us, his dear offspring? It cannot be that he has failed. If he had met with disaster, he would have returned by now, driven back in fury by his pursuers, since no place suits his punishment or their vengeance like this one.

I feel new strength rising within me, wings growing, and a dominion given me beyond this deep. Whatever draws me -- whether sympathy or some innate force powerful enough to unite things of like nature across any distance through secret attraction -- you, my inseparable shadow, must come with me.

For Death cannot be separated from Sin. But lest the difficulty of passing back over this impassable, impervious gulf delay his return, let us try an adventurous work, not beyond our combined power: to build a path over this vast main from Hell to that new world where Satan now prevails. This will be a glorious monument to all the infernal host, easing their passage back and forth for visits or migration, as their fortunes direct.

Nor can I miss the way, so strongly drawn by this new attraction and instinct." The gaunt Shadow answered quickly: "Go wherever Fate and strong inclination lead you. I shall not lag behind or lose the way while you lead. I catch such a scent of carnage and innumerable prey, and taste the flavor of death from all living things there.

Nor shall I be unhelpful in the work you undertake. I shall provide equal assistance." So saying, he sniffed with delight the smell of mortal change wafting from Earth. Like a flock of ravenous birds that, though many leagues away, flies toward a battlefield on the eve of combat, drawn by the scent of living bodies destined for death in the next day's bloody fight --

so this grim figure sniffed the air, its nostrils flaring wide in the murky atmosphere, tracking its quarry from afar. Then both flew from Hell's gates into the vast, chaotic waste of damp, dark Chaos. With great power -- their power was immense -- they hovered over the waters. Whatever they found solid or slimy, tossed up and down as in a raging sea, they drove together and shoved toward the mouth of Hell.

Like two polar winds blowing from opposite sides and driving mountains of ice together on the Arctic Sea until they block the imagined passage to the rich coasts of China -- so they worked. Death, with his club-like weapon, cold and dry, struck the collected soil and fixed it solid as the island Delos that once floated. The rest he froze with his Gorgon-like gaze so it could not move.

With tar-like slime, as wide as the gate of Hell and deep to its very roots, they fastened the gathered material and built an enormous causeway. It arched high over the foaming deep, a prodigious bridge connecting to the now-defenseless wall of this world, which was forfeit to Death. From there, a broad, smooth, easy, harmless passage led down to Hell.

To compare great things with small: so Xerxes, seeking to yoke the freedom of Greece, came from Susa and his great palace, bridging the Hellespont to join Europe with Asia, scourging the indignant waves with many a stroke.

Now Sin and Death had brought their marvelous work of engineering -- a ridge of hanging rock over the troubled abyss -- all the way along Satan's track to the very spot where he first landed from his flight out of Chaos, on the bare outside of this round world. With pins of adamant and chains they secured it -- all too firmly, all too permanently! And now the borders of heavenly Heaven, this World, and Hell (on the left hand) all met in a small space, with three separate ways leading to each of the three places.

Now they could see their way to Earth, heading first toward Paradise. But suddenly Satan appeared, disguised as a bright angel, steering between the constellations of the Centaur and the Scorpion while the Sun rose in Aries.

He came in disguise, but his children quickly recognized their parent despite the deception. After seducing Eve, he had slunk unseen into the nearby woods. Changing shape to observe the aftermath, he watched his deceitful scheme succeed as Eve unknowingly led Adam to the same act. He saw their shame as they sought useless covering. But when he saw the Son of God descend to judge them, he fled in terror -- not hoping to escape, but only to avoid the present moment, fearing what immediate punishment God's anger might inflict. Once that passed, he returned by night. Listening to the unhappy couple's sorrowful conversation, he gathered his own doom from their words. Understanding that the sentence was not immediate but postponed to the future, he returned to Hell with joy and promising news.

At the edge of Chaos, near the foot of this new and wondrous bridge, he unexpectedly met his offspring, who had come to meet him. Great joy was shared at their meeting, and the sight of that tremendous bridge increased his delight.

He stood admiring it for a long time, until Sin, his fair enchanting daughter, broke the silence: "O Father, these are your magnificent achievements, your trophies! You see them as though they are not yours, but you are their author and chief architect.

For no sooner did my heart sense -- and my heart, through a secret harmony, always moves in tune with yours, joined in sweet connection -- that you had prospered on Earth, which your expression now confirms as well, than immediately, though worlds apart, I felt that I must follow you with your son.

Such fatal connection unites the three of us! Hell could no longer contain us. Neither could this impassable gulf keep us from following your glorious trail. You have won our freedom, previously confined within Hell's gates. You have empowered us to build this far and bridge the dark abyss with this tremendous structure.

All this world is now yours. Your wisdom has won what your weapons lost in war, fully avenging our defeat in Heaven. Here you shall rule as monarch. There let the other one continue to rule, as battle decided. He retreats from this new world, alienated by his own decree,

and henceforth divides the monarchy with you, separated by the boundaries of Heaven from your spherical domain. Or perhaps you may try something even more dangerous to his throne." The Prince of Darkness answered gladly.

"Fair daughter, and you, my son and grandchild both -- you have given high proof of being truly Satan's offspring (for I glory in the name of Antagonist to Heaven's Almighty King). You have amply earned merit from me and from the whole infernal empire by meeting me with this triumphant work at the very doorstep of Heaven itself -- your triumph joined with mine. You have made one realm, one continent, of Hell and this world, with easy passage between them. Therefore, while I descend through darkness on your well-built road to my fellow Powers to share these successes and rejoice with them,

you two, follow this way among these countless spheres -- all yours now -- straight down to Paradise. Dwell there and rule in bliss. Exercise dominion on Earth and in the air, chiefly over Man, who is declared sole lord of everything.

First make him your slave, and finally kill him. I send you as my deputies and create you plenipotentiaries on Earth, with matchless power issuing from me. My hold on this new kingdom depends entirely on your combined strength -- through Sin, Man is exposed to Death by my doing.

If your joint power prevails, Hell's affairs need fear no harm. Go, and be strong!" With these words he sent them on their way. They sped through the thickest constellations, spreading their blight. The blasted stars looked pale, and the planets, planet-struck, suffered a real eclipse. Satan went the other way, down the causeway to Hell's gate. On either side, Chaos, driven back, surged against the bridge but could not break it. Through the gate, wide open and unguarded, Satan passed. He found the area around the gate deserted, for those assigned to guard it had abandoned their post and flown up to the world above. The rest had withdrawn far inland, around the walls of Pandemonium -- the city and proud seat of Lucifer, named by allusion after that same bright star whose parallel Satan was.

The legions there kept watch while the high council sat in session, anxiously wondering what chance might befall their emperor, whom they had sent forth. He had given this command before departing, and they obeyed. Like a Tartar army retreating from its Russian enemy past Astrakhan over the snowy plains, or a Persian king falling back from the Turkish crescent beyond the realm of Aladule to Tabriz or Isfahan, these Heaven-banished exiles had abandoned the outer reaches of Hell and gathered in careful watch around their capital. They waited hourly for their great adventurer's return from his search of foreign worlds. He passed through their midst unrecognized, disguised as a common angel of the lowest order. From the door of that Plutonian hall, he ascended invisible to his high throne, which was placed in regal splendor beneath a rich canopy at the upper end. For a while he sat there, looking around unseen at the assembly.

Then at last, as if from a cloud, his radiant head and star-bright form appeared, clad in whatever glory was left to him since his fall, or perhaps just false glitter. All were amazed at the sudden blaze. The assembly turned and saw whom they had hoped to see -- their mighty chief returned. The applause was loud.

The great consulting lords rushed forward eagerly, raised from their dark council. They approached him with congratulatory joy. He silenced them with his hand and won their attention with these words: "Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, Virtues, Powers!

I call you by these titles as possessions held in fact, not merely in right. I have returned, successful beyond hope, to lead you forth triumphant out of this infernal pit -- this abominable, accursed house of misery and dungeon of our tyrant. Now take possession as lords of a spacious world, not much inferior to our native Heaven, achieved by my hard and perilous adventure. It would take too long to describe everything I have done, suffered, and endured -- voyaging the unreal, vast, unbounded deep of horrible confusion. Over it, Sin and Death have now paved a broad highway to speed your glorious march. But I blazed the original trail through that untamable abyss, forced to ride the trackless chaos of primal Night.

Night and Chaos, jealous of their secrets, fiercely opposed my strange journey with a clamorous uproar, protesting supreme Fate. Then I found the newly created world, long prophesied in Heaven -- an absolutely perfect work of creation! There Man was placed in a Paradise, made happy by our exile. By fraud I have seduced him from his Creator. And -- to increase your wonder -- I did it with an apple! God, offended -- and this should make you laugh! -- has given up both his beloved Man and his entire world to Sin and Death as prey, and to us, without any risk, effort, or alarm on our part.

Ours to roam in, to dwell in, and to rule over Man as over everything he was meant to rule. True, he has also judged me -- or rather, not me but the brute serpent in whose form I deceived Man. The part concerning me is this: enmity between me and humanity. I am to bruise his heel.

His offspring -- the time not specified -- shall bruise my head. Who would not buy a world for a bruise, or even for much worse pain? You have heard my report. What remains, gods, but to rise and enter into full enjoyment of your bliss?"

Having said this, he stood for a moment, expecting the universal shout and loud applause to fill his ear. Instead, to the contrary, he heard from every side a universal hiss from innumerable tongues -- the sound of public contempt. He was astonished, but his astonishment at the reaction was quickly overtaken by astonishment at himself. He felt his face sharpen and narrow.

His arms clung to his ribs. His legs twisted around each other until, toppled from his feet, he fell prone -- a monstrous serpent on his belly, struggling but powerless. A greater power now ruled him, punishing him in the very form in which he had sinned, according to his sentence. He tried to speak, but his words came out as hisses. His forked tongue could produce nothing but hissing sounds, for now all his followers were transformed alike into serpents -- accessories to his bold crime. Terrifying was the sound of hissing that filled the hall as they swarmed, now thick with tangled monsters, heads and tails intertwined: scorpions, asps, amphisbaenas, horned cerastes, water snakes, and dipsas serpents. But still the greatest among them, in the middle, now grown into a dragon -- larger than the great Python engendered by the sun in the Pythian vale -- Satan seemed to retain his power above the rest. They all followed him, pouring out into the open field where the rest of the fallen host, those who had not been inside, stood in formation or arranged for battle.

They stood with high expectation, ready to see their glorious chief emerge in triumph. Instead they saw something quite different -- a crowd of hideous serpents! Horror fell upon them, and a dreadful sympathy, for what they saw they felt happening to themselves. They too were changing. Down fell their weapons -- both spear and shield -- and down they fell just as quickly.

The terrible hissing renewed as the dire form spread by contagion, punishment matching crime. Their intended applause turned to hissing disgrace, triumph to shame cast from their own mouths. Nearby, a grove sprang up as part of their transformation -- God's will, to increase their punishment. It was laden with fair fruit like that which grew in Paradise, the very bait Eve had fallen for. At this strange prospect, they fixed their eager eyes, imagining that instead of one forbidden tree, a multitude had now risen to bring them further misery or shame.

Yet, scorched with burning thirst and fierce hunger -- though the fruit was sent only to mock them -- they could not resist. They rolled in heaps toward the trees, climbing up and sitting thicker than the snaky locks that curled on Medusa's head. Greedily they plucked the fruit, which looked fair, like the legendary fruit that grew near the bituminous lake where Sodom had flamed.

But this was even more deceptive. Not the touch but the taste betrayed them. Expecting to satisfy their appetite with flavor, they found only bitter ashes instead of fruit. The offended taste spat out the gritty, sooty mouthful with a spattering noise. Again and again they tried, driven by hunger and thirst. Again and again they were punished with the same hateful, disgusting taste, their jaws writhing with soot and cinders. So they were plagued, worn down by famine and endless hissing, until finally they were permitted to resume their lost shapes.

Some say this humiliation was imposed on them for a certain number of days each year, to crush their pride and punish their joy over Man's seduction. However, they spread some traditions among the pagan world about their conquest, telling of how the Serpent -- whom the Greeks called Ophion -- along with Eurynome, perhaps representing the wide-ranging Eve, had first ruled high Olympus, before being driven out by Saturn and Ops, even before Dictaean Jove was born.

Meanwhile, in Paradise, the hellish pair arrived all too soon -- Sin, now present in body to dwell as a permanent resident (she had been there before only in effect), with Death close behind, pace for pace, not yet mounted on his pale horse. Sin spoke to Death.

"Second child of Satan, all-conquering Death! What do you think of our empire now? Hard-earned by difficult travel, but far better than still sitting at Hell's dark threshold as an unnamed, undreaded, half-starved watchman?"

The monster born of Sin replied: "To me, who suffer eternal hunger, Hell, Paradise, or Heaven are all the same. Wherever I can find the most to devour is best. Here, though the pickings seem plentiful, this vast, unfillable body finds them barely enough.

To which the incestuous mother replied: "Then start with these herbs, fruits, and flowers. Then move on to every beast, fish, and bird -- no humble morsels! And whatever the scythe of Time mows down, devour without sparing.

Until I, dwelling within Man, infect his entire race through their thoughts, looks, words, and actions, seasoning him as your last and sweetest prey." Having said this, they both went their separate ways, each to destroy or make mortal all living kinds, hastening them toward destruction sooner or later. The Almighty, seeing this from his heavenly seat among the saints, spoke to those bright orders.

"See how eagerly these dogs of Hell advance to waste and ravage that world which I created so fair and good, and which would still be in that state had not the folly of Man let these devastating forces in. They blame me for their entry, as does the Prince of Hell and his followers, claiming that I too easily permitted them to enter and possess such a heavenly place, seemingly allowing it, as if in a fit of passion I had carelessly yielded everything to their misrule.

But they do not know that I called and drew these Hell-hounds here to lick up the filth and refuse that Man's polluting sin has shed on what was pure. When they are crammed and gorged, nearly bursting with the swallowed offal, a single stroke of your victorious arm, beloved Son, shall hurl both Sin and Death, along with the yawning Grave, through Chaos and seal up Hell's ravenous jaws forever.

Then Heaven and Earth, renewed and purified, shall receive no more stain until then. The curse already pronounced on both now takes effect." He ended, and the heavenly audience sang a loud Hallelujah, like the sound of seas through the multitude that sang: "Just are your ways, righteous are your decrees upon all your works!"

"Who can diminish you?" Then they sang to the Son, the destined Restorer of humanity, through whom new Heavens and a new Earth shall rise or descend from Heaven. Such was their song. Meanwhile the Creator, calling his mighty angels by name, gave each of them specific assignments suited to the present circumstances. The Sun was given instructions on how to move and shine so as to affect the Earth with cold and heat barely tolerable -- calling harsh winter from the north and scorching summer heat from the south. He prescribed the Moon's duties and gave the other five planets their motions and aspects -- in every combination: favorable and unfavorable, harmonious and hostile. He taught the fixed stars when to shed their malignant influence. He assigned the winds their corners, telling them when to blow and confuse sea, air, and shore with storms. He directed the thunder when to roll with terror through the dark sky.

Some say he commanded his angels to tilt the Earth's axis more than twenty degrees from alignment with the Sun. Others say the Sun was directed to turn its path away from the equator, traveling as far as the Tropic of Cancer past Taurus and the Pleiades and the Twins, then back down through Leo, Virgo, and Libra to Capricorn -- introducing the change of seasons to every region. Otherwise, perpetual spring would have smiled on the Earth with green flowers, equal in days and nights, except in the polar regions where the low sun would have circled continuously, unknown of east or west, keeping snow from the northlands and preventing scorching in the south. But after Man tasted the forbidden fruit, the Sun turned from its intended course. How else could the world, even if sinless, have avoided the extremes of freezing cold and scorching heat?

These changes in the heavens, though gradual, produced similar changes on sea and land -- destructive blasts, vapors, mists, and hot, pestilent exhalations. Now from the north came Boreas and other fierce winds, bursting from their frozen dungeons armed with ice, snow, hail, and stormy gusts, tearing at forests and churning up seas.

From the south, equally fierce, came the hot winds -- Notus and Afer, black with thunderclouds from Sierra Leone. From east and west, Eurus and Zephyr clashed with their sideways blasts, along with Sirocco and Libecchio. So violence began even among lifeless things. But Discord, Daughter of Sin, first introduced Death among the irrational animals through fierce mutual hatred.

Beast now made war on beast, bird on bird, fish on fish. They abandoned grazing on plants and devoured each other. They no longer stood in awe of Man but fled from him, or else glared at him with threatening looks as he passed. These were the external miseries that Adam saw, already in part. Though hidden in the deepest gloom, he felt even worse things stirring within himself.

Tossed in a troubled sea of passion, he sought to unburden himself with this sad complaint: "O miserable reversal of happiness! Is this the end of this new, glorious world -- and me, so recently the glory of that glory, now become accursed instead of blessed? Hide me from the face of God, whose sight was once the height of my happiness! Yet, if only the misery would end here. I deserved it and would bear my own punishment.

But all that I eat, drink, or shall produce is a transmitted curse. O voice, once heard with delight: 'Be fruitful and multiply!' Now it is death to hear! For what can I increase or multiply but curses on my own head?

Who of all future ages, feeling the evil I brought upon them, will not curse my name? 'We can thank our ancestor for this ill fortune!' they will say. Their thanks will be curses. So on top of my own guilt that stays with me, all humanity's curses shall rebound on me like a fierce flood --

all coming to rest on me as on their natural center, heavy though settled in their proper place. O fleeting joys of Paradise, purchased at the price of lasting woe! Did I ask you, Maker, to mold me from clay into a man? Did I petition you to lift me from darkness and place me in this delightful garden? Since my will did not consent to my own being, it would be only right and fair to reduce me back to dust,

willing as I am to resign and return everything I received. Unable to meet your terms, which were too hard for me to fulfill, I should not be held to the good I never sought. Is losing that good not sufficient punishment? Why have you added the sense of endless misery? Your justice seems inexplicable. Yet -- I confess it too late -- I should have refused those terms when they were first offered.

You accepted them. Will you enjoy the good and then object to the conditions? And though God made you without your permission, what if your own son proved disobedient and, when rebuked, retorted: 'Why did you create me? I never asked for it!' Would you accept such an arrogant excuse? Yet his was not your choice but natural necessity.

God made you by his own free choice to serve him. Your reward was from his grace. Your punishment, then, is justly his to determine. So be it. I submit. His judgment is fair: that I am dust and shall return to dust.

O welcome hour, whenever it comes! Why does his hand delay carrying out what his decree has fixed for this very day? Why do I go on living? Why am I mocked with death and stretched out in deathless pain? How gladly would I meet my death sentence and become senseless earth! How gladly I would lie down as in my mother's lap and sleep secure! His dreadful voice would thunder in my ears no more. No fear of worse to come for me or my descendants would torment me with cruel expectation. Yet one doubt pursues me still: perhaps not all of me can die.

Perhaps that pure breath of life, the spirit of Man, which God inspired, cannot perish together with this body of clay. Then in the grave, or in some other dismal place, I might die a living death.
